---
date: 2026-04-22
time: 09:00 PT (scheduled 60 min, ran 75 min, ended 10:15 PT)
location: Zoom (Coppertide tenant)
recording: enabled, auto-transcribed; this file is a cleaned pass over the auto-transcript with timestamps approximate to the nearest minute
attendees:
  - Priya Iyer (Orbital, co-founder, lead consultant) — host
  - Marcus Lehrer (Orbital, co-founder, architect) — Berlin, joined at 09:00, 18:00 local
  - Devansh Mehta (Coppertide, CTO)
  - Aria Tan (Coppertide, Head of Analytics)
  - Quentin Reyes (Coppertide, Data Engineer) — joined 09:10 after a deploy
  - Lina Costa (Coppertide, VP Marketing) — left 09:45 for board prep
notes_taker: Priya (live), cleaned by Marcus same evening
---

# Coppertide x Orbital — Engagement Kickoff

## Transcript

**[09:00]**

**Priya:** Morning, everyone. I see Devansh and Aria. Marcus, you there?

**Marcus:** I'm here. Hi from Berlin. It's six in the evening so if I sound a bit slow that's why.

**Priya:** Lina, hi — I see you joined. Quentin's not on yet?

**Devansh:** He's mid-deploy. He pinged me five minutes ago, said he'd be ten minutes late. We can start without him; he mostly needs to listen.

**Priya:** Okay. So — thanks again for making time. The plan for today, just to set the frame, is: I want to spend about fifteen minutes on context, where you are today, what's working, what isn't. Then we'll talk about what the engagement actually looks like — phases, cadence, who owns what. And then we leave time at the end for questions and access logistics, because there's some boring SOC stuff we need to nail down. Sound okay?

**Devansh:** Sounds good.

**Aria:** Yep, works for me.

**Priya:** Great. Marcus, do you want to do the thirty-second on us?

**Marcus:** Sure. So Orbital — Priya and I started it about three years ago after we both left, well, separate places. We do data infrastructure consulting for Series B and C companies, mostly DTC and marketplaces. We're not — we don't try to be a managed service. We come in, we audit, we fix the worst things, we set you up so your team can run it, and then we leave. The number we care about is whether your internal team is faster six months after we're gone. Not whether you've renewed with us.

**Priya:** Yeah, and I think for context — Devansh and I talked about this a couple of times before, but Aria and Lina, you may not have heard it — the typical engagement is twelve weeks. We've done shorter and we've done longer. Twelve has been the right number for the kind of "we've outgrown our setup but haven't broken it yet" stage that — honestly — sounds a lot like where you are.

**Devansh:** Yeah. That's a fair description.

**[09:04]**

**Priya:** Okay. So let's do the context. Devansh, I've got notes from our prep call — I don't want to put words in your mouth, so why don't you walk us through where you think the data stack is, and then Aria and Lina please jump in wherever it's wrong or incomplete.

**Devansh:** Sure. So — high level. We're about eighty people, we crossed forty million ARR last quarter, growing about thirty-five percent year over year. Most of our revenue is DTC cookware, Shopify Plus is our storefront, we've got a small wholesale business that we're not going to talk about today because it doesn't really touch the data stack. Headquarters in New York, warehouse in Reno, and the office is hybrid — Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday in person.

**Priya:** And the stack?

**Devansh:** The stack. So. Production database is Postgres on RDS. We have Snowflake — Standard tier — that we use for analytics. Stitch for ingestion. dbt Cloud for transformations. Looker for dashboards. Segment for events. That's basically it.

**Aria:** You forgot Klaviyo.

**Devansh:** Klaviyo is a source, not part of the stack proper. But yes, Klaviyo is where our email events live and we pull them through Stitch.

**Priya:** Okay. And of those — what's working and what isn't?

**Devansh:** Honestly, all of it works in the sense that data flows through it and the dashboards mostly aren't on fire. But we've outgrown three pieces of it.

**Priya:** Walk me through.

**Devansh:** One — Stitch. Our April invoice was two thousand and thirty-four dollars. I have it open. (laughs) Two thousand and thirty-four. Last April we paid like nine hundred. The pricing page is — sorry — the Stitch pricing page is genuinely incomprehensible to me. I have a CS degree. I cannot tell you what we are paying for.

**Marcus:** I will say, in Stitch's defense — and I am not trying to defend Stitch here — every ingestion vendor's pricing page is incomprehensible. Fivetran's is also bad. They're all bad.

**Devansh:** Fine. But on top of that, we're hitting row-count limits on one of our streams. The Klaviyo events stream. It's about fourteen million rows a day right now, and Stitch keeps throttling it, which means our email engagement metrics are eight to ten hours stale by the time Aria's team looks at them in the morning.

**Aria:** It used to be four hours. It got worse after Spring Pans.

**Priya:** Spring Pans?

**Aria:** Our April campaign. The launch went live April third. Email volume basically tripled for ten days, and the Klaviyo events firehose just — we never came back down to baseline because we kept the segmentation cadence high.

**Devansh:** Right. So Stitch is squeezing us on two axes. Cost is up and reliability is down. I want to evaluate alternatives. Before this call I would have said Fivetran or build our own Postgres CDC pipeline. I have — I'll be honest — I have strong opinions about owning the ingestion layer for compliance reasons. We have a SOC 2 audit coming up. I'll get into it later.

**Priya:** Okay, we'll come back to that. What's the second thing?

**[09:09]**

**Devansh:** Second is dbt. Aria, you want to take this one?

**Aria:** Yeah. So our dbt Cloud project is — it works. We have, what, two production models? Quentin would know better. But the project is undocumented. There are no descriptions. There are no tests. The lineage graph in dbt Docs is a mess because half the sources aren't declared. Quentin and I are the only two people in the company who can change anything in there safely. And we want to hire a marketing analyst —

**[09:10]**

**Quentin:** Hi, sorry, sorry, I'm here. Deploy went sideways.

**Devansh:** Did it land?

**Quentin:** Yeah, it landed. Just the canary was being weird. Sorry, please continue.

**Aria:** I was saying — we want to hire a marketing analyst. We have a candidate we like. But onboarding her is going to take, like, six weeks instead of two, because the only way to learn our dbt setup is for Quentin or me to sit next to her and explain why model X depends on model Y. There's no documentation. There's no semantic layer. There's no — like, we don't even have a glossary of metrics.

**Priya:** Bus factor of two.

**Aria:** Bus factor of two. And I'm taking three weeks off in August so really it's a bus factor of one for that window.

**Quentin:** (quietly) I am aware.

**Devansh:** And then the third thing, which is really Lina's, is the dashboards.

**Lina:** Oh, do you want me to —

**Devansh:** Yeah, go.

**Lina:** Okay. So. I have been hand-reconciling our weekly revenue numbers between marketing and finance for two months. Every Monday morning. The marketing dashboard in Looker says one number for paid revenue and the finance dashboard says a different number. Sometimes they're off by half a percent. Sometimes they're off by eight percent. Last week it was four point two percent. I want to — can I share my screen for a second? I want to show you something.

**Priya:** Please.

**Lina:** Okay, you should be seeing — this is our marketing dashboard. This is "paid revenue last week." The number is four hundred and twelve thousand, six hundred and something. Now I'm going to pull up the finance dashboard. Same week. (pause) Three hundred and ninety-six thousand. Same definition, supposedly. Same data warehouse. Different number.

**Marcus:** And do you know why?

**Lina:** I know it's something to do with how attribution windows are defined and how refunds get netted, but I have asked four times for a written definition of "paid revenue" and I have gotten four different answers. Two of them were from the same person.

**Aria:** That person was me. In my defense, the definition changed.

**Lina:** (laughs) Yes, that is the problem.

**Priya:** This is — okay, this is exactly the kind of thing that a semantic layer is supposed to solve. We'll talk about it. Aria, what do you wish for? If you could wave a wand.

**Aria:** Honestly? I want one Looker dashboard that the C-team agrees on for our Monday business review. One. Just one. I don't even need it to be pretty. I need everyone in that room to look at the same number and not argue about whether it's right.

**Lina:** Plus one to that.

**Devansh:** Plus one.

**Priya:** Got it. Okay. Anything else on pain points before I go through what we'd do about it?

**Devansh:** One more thing. Snowflake. We're paying about eight hundred a month for it and it is — I would estimate — ten percent utilized. The warehouse is on Standard tier. We bought it eighteen months ago thinking we'd be doing real analytics by now and we mostly aren't. So that's a "we're paying for capacity we're not using" problem rather than a "things are broken" problem, but it's annoying.

**Marcus:** Standard tier is fine for your size, by the way. Don't downgrade impulsively. The cost of switching tiers later is — it's not the dollars, it's the calendar time.

**Devansh:** Noted.

**Priya:** Looker license — you mentioned it on our prep call?

**Devansh:** Fourteen hundred a month. Four creator seats. We have like fifteen viewers. The seats are actually fine. The seats are not the issue.

**Priya:** Okay, good. Just wanted to anchor the cost numbers. So you're paying — roughly — two thousand for ingestion, eight hundred for warehouse, fourteen hundred for BI. Plus dbt Cloud, plus Segment.

**Devansh:** dbt Cloud is — I think it's a hundred a seat? We have three. And Segment is, ugh, I don't have it in my head, but it's the smallest line item.

**Priya:** Okay. Tiny aside but useful — I'll send a worksheet later this week where we put all of it in one place, with last twelve months of spend per tool, and we project forward at current growth. Useful for Phase 3 conversations.

**[09:18]**

**Priya:** Okay, let me walk through what I think the engagement looks like. This is a draft. Push back on anything.

**Priya:** Twelve weeks, four phases of three weeks each.

**Priya:** Phase one, weeks one through three: audit and document. That means we sit with Quentin and Aria, walk through every model in dbt, every dashboard in Looker, every Stitch source. We write the documentation that doesn't exist. We don't change anything yet. We're just creating the map. Output is a written document — probably forty to fifty pages — plus a populated dbt project with descriptions and basic tests on the critical models. Plus a glossary of metrics, which is actually the most important deliverable.

**Aria:** The glossary is the dream.

**Priya:** The glossary is, in some ways, the whole engagement. Phase two, weeks four through six: we build the semantic layer and lock down canonical definitions. So "paid revenue" gets defined once, in one place, in code, with tests. Same with organic revenue, AOV, repeat rate, all the headline metrics. We use Looker's modeling layer for this — LookML — because you already have Looker. We're not going to introduce a new tool here.

**Lina:** Thank god.

**Priya:** Phase three, weeks seven through nine: this is the ingestion evaluation. We do a real, structured comparison of Fivetran versus building our own Postgres CDC pipeline. We benchmark on cost at your current volume, cost projection at year-plus-one volume, reliability, and SOC 2 fit. We do not — Devansh, this is per our pre-call — we do not include Airbyte in the evaluation. Confirm?

**Devansh:** Confirmed. Airbyte is too immature for what we need. I don't want to spend cycles on it.

**Priya:** Got it. And phase four, weeks ten through twelve: handoff and training. We document everything we did, we run training sessions with Quentin and Aria and whoever else needs to know, and we hand the keys back. Done.

**Devansh:** That all sounds — yeah. That tracks.

**Aria:** I have a question on phase three.

**Priya:** Go.

**Aria:** Are we going to — like — actually swap Stitch out during phase three? Or just decide what to swap it to?

**Priya:** Just decide. The migration itself would be a separate engagement, or you do it yourselves. Three weeks is not enough to evaluate, decide, and migrate. It's enough to evaluate and decide and write the migration plan.

**Aria:** Okay. Good. I was nervous you were going to try to migrate in three weeks.

**Priya:** No, no. That would be — no.

**[09:24]**

**Marcus:** Can I add one thing on phase two?

**Priya:** Please.

**Marcus:** I want to — and this is just me thinking out loud, not a recommendation yet — but I want to flag that for greenfield semantic layer work I have been increasingly using SQLMesh instead of dbt. Especially when there's no existing dbt sprawl. Coppertide has a small dbt project, two production models, so it's not totally locked in. Just — I want to put the option on the table.

**Aria:** Hmm.

**Quentin:** I have feelings.

**Aria:** Quentin, go.

**Quentin:** We just got everyone — and by everyone I mean me and you, Aria, and the two backend engineers who occasionally write models — we just got everyone to learn dbt. We had a six-week internal effort last fall to get the team comfortable. Switching to SQLMesh now would feel like — I don't want to say a betrayal, but —

**Aria:** A betrayal. Yeah. Plus the talent pool. We can hire dbt people. SQLMesh is still rare.

**Marcus:** That's fair. Both of those are legitimate. I'm not going to push it. I just wanted to name it so we don't end the engagement and you find out a year later that the option existed.

**Priya:** Let's defer this. We don't have to decide on the call. Mark it as an open question and we'll revisit it during phase one when we see what the dbt project actually looks like.

**Devansh:** Agreed. Park it.

**[09:27]**

**Priya:** Okay. SOC 2. Devansh, you want to — what's the requirement?

**Devansh:** Yes. So. We have a SOC 2 Type 2 audit starting — well, the observation window starts July first. We need to have controls in place before then. The hard requirement that's relevant to this engagement: any vendor in our data path that processes PII has to keep that processing in the United States. No EU routing. Specifically because some of our European customers — we're treating their data under our US framework with consent, but the auditor was very clear that we cannot have data crossing back to EU infra and then forward to US infra. It has to be US-only.

**Priya:** Okay. So that's a constraint on Fivetran in particular — Fivetran has multiple regions and you'd need to make sure you're on US.

**Devansh:** Yes. And it's a constraint on Stitch, currently, that we already validated. Stitch's US region is fine.

**Priya:** Got it. We'll bake that into the phase three eval as a hard filter, not a soft one.

**Devansh:** Also — and this is the thing I wanted to ask you about — can you send us a draft data-handling addendum? Something we can append to our contract that covers PII processing scope, retention, data location. The auditor specifically asked whether our consultants had one.

**Priya:** Yes. I'll send a draft within a week. Call it — by next Wednesday. April twenty-ninth.

**Devansh:** Perfect.

**[09:31]**

**Priya:** Okay, let's talk cadence. I want to do a weekly review, sixty minutes, where we look at what got done last week, what's planned for next week, and any blockers. I was going to propose Friday at ten AM Pacific. That's one PM Eastern, seven PM Berlin.

**Aria:** Can we move it?

**Priya:** Sure, what works?

**Aria:** Friday is when we deploy. We do a one PM Eastern deploy basically every Friday. If something goes wrong I need to be in the deploy, and I will be useless on a review call. Can we do Thursday afternoon?

**Priya:** Thursday at one PM Eastern? That's ten AM Pacific, seven PM Berlin. Marcus, that work for you?

**Marcus:** Seven PM Berlin is fine. I would prefer six but seven is fine.

**Aria:** Thursday one PM Eastern works for me.

**Devansh:** Works for me.

**Priya:** Quentin?

**Quentin:** Yeah, fine.

**Priya:** Lina, do you want to be on these?

**Lina:** I — honestly, probably not weekly. Can I get the notes and join when there's a marketing-relevant item?

**Priya:** Absolutely. Okay so first review is — let's see, Thursday — that would be next week, April thirtieth. One PM Eastern. I'll send the invite.

**Aria:** April thirtieth. Got it.

**[09:35]**

**Priya:** Access. We're going to need read-only access to Looker, dbt Cloud, and Snowflake for me and Marcus. Read-only is fine for phase one. Phase two we'll need write to dbt and write to LookML. Phase three we'll scope separately.

**Aria:** I can do read-only by end of day today. It's all SAML, I just need to add you to the right groups.

**Priya:** Today is great. I'll send our work emails right after this call.

**Devansh:** Quentin, you'll need to grant Snowflake. Aria can do Looker and dbt Cloud.

**Quentin:** Yeah, I'll spin up roles for them this afternoon. ANALYST_RO or similar. Standard tier doesn't give us a ton of granularity but it's enough.

**Marcus:** Standard tier is fine for read-only. We don't need the fancy stuff.

**[09:38]**

**Priya:** Okay. Let me ask the awkward question. What are you afraid of? With this engagement.

**Devansh:** (pause) Honestly? I'm afraid we'll spend twelve weeks documenting and end up with a beautiful audit and the same problems. I've seen consultants do that. They produce a deck and leave.

**Priya:** Yeah. That's fair. The way we try to address that is — the deliverables in phase one are not a deck. The deliverable is a populated dbt project and a glossary in a wiki. It's stuff that lives in your tools, not in our slides. If we leave and there's a Notion page you'll never open again, we've failed.

**Devansh:** Okay.

**Aria:** I'm afraid Quentin and I will not have time to support you. We are very busy.

**Priya:** That's the realest answer. Honestly, the engagement only works if we can get — call it three to four hours a week of your time, Aria, and probably four to six of Quentin's, especially in phases one and three. If you can't give us that, we should know now.

**Aria:** I can do four. Quentin, six?

**Quentin:** I can do six if it's spread out and not on Fridays.

**Marcus:** Not on Fridays. Got it.

**Lina:** Can I add one?

**Priya:** Please.

**Lina:** I'm afraid we'll define "paid revenue" in a way that, when I look at it next year, I disagree with. And then we'll have the same problem again, just with our own rules instead of vendor defaults.

**Priya:** That is a real risk. The way we mitigate is — the definitions get reviewed by you, by Aria, and by whoever owns finance, before they ship. We don't ship a definition that the relevant stakeholder hasn't signed off on. And we make the review process repeatable so when it changes — and it will change — there's a path to change it cleanly.

**Lina:** Okay. Yeah. That helps.

**[09:43]**

**Lina:** I have to drop in two minutes for board prep. Before I go — one thing.

**Priya:** Go.

**Lina:** I want to flag — I've informally seen dashboards from a competitor of ours, Hearth and Iron. Through a former colleague. I'm not going to send them around because they're not mine to share, but their methodology on what they call "earned revenue" is — it's really clean. They distinguish paid, organic, and what they call earned, which is essentially repeat purchases that originate from non-paid touchpoints. I'd love for us to look at something like that. I don't know if it makes sense for our scale.

**Priya:** Noted. I'll think about it. We don't have to copy their taxonomy, but if there's a useful distinction in there we can borrow it.

**Lina:** Cool. Okay, I have to run. Thanks everyone, this was — this was actually really useful.

**Priya:** Thanks Lina, talk soon.

**[09:45 — Lina leaves]**

**[09:46]**

**Priya:** Okay, with Lina off — Quentin, you've been quiet. Anything you want to flag that you didn't want to say in front of Lina?

**Quentin:** (pause) Yeah, actually, one thing. On Fivetran specifically. We tried Fivetran in 2024. Briefly. Like, three weeks.

**Priya:** Oh.

**Quentin:** And we hit an issue with the Shopify Plus connector. It was pulling duplicate orders. We — I mean — the symptom was that orders with line-item edits would come through twice, once as the original and once as the edit, but with the same order ID and overlapping timestamps. Our downstream models exploded. We rolled back to Stitch and never tried again.

**Marcus:** Was that with their then-current Shopify Plus connector or the legacy one?

**Quentin:** I think it was — I don't actually remember. It was August 2024.

**Marcus:** Okay. Fair to say it might be fixed now. They rewrote that connector, I think, late 2024 or early 2025. But we should validate it specifically before we recommend anything.

**Devansh:** Yeah, that's a good catch, Quentin. I forgot we tried them.

**Quentin:** I figured I should mention it.

**Priya:** Thank you. That changes phase three a little — we should specifically include a duplicate-order test in the Shopify Plus connector evaluation. Not a deal-breaker but a known risk we should test for.

**[09:50]**

**Devansh:** What about the custom CDC option? Walk me through how you'd evaluate that.

**Priya:** Marcus, you want to take this?

**Marcus:** Sure. So custom CDC for Postgres usually means one of two stacks. Either Debezium plus Kafka plus a sink into Snowflake, or you skip Kafka and use something like Estuary or you write a thinner consumer yourself. For Coppertide's volume — what is it, Quentin, your Postgres write volume?

**Quentin:** Maybe — twenty to thirty megabytes per second on a peak day? Most days less.

**Marcus:** That's not a lot. You don't need Kafka. You could probably do this with a fairly thin Debezium-to-Snowflake pipeline, maybe a hundred lines of glue code, and the operational burden is — it's real but it's manageable. Two engineers can own it.

**Devansh:** And the SOC 2 fit?

**Marcus:** Custom CDC is the cleanest SOC 2 fit because you control every hop. There's no third party processing the data. The downside is you own the pager when it breaks.

**Devansh:** Right.

**Marcus:** I want to be honest — I don't think we should pre-commit to one direction. The phase three evaluation should be real. Cost, reliability, fit, team capacity. If Fivetran on US region with the new Shopify connector works, it might be the right answer even if you have a philosophical preference for owning ingestion. And if the build looks like the right answer, we'll know that too.

**Devansh:** Fair.

**[09:55]**

**Priya:** Okay, I want to be conscious of time. We're scheduled for sixty minutes and I'm going to push us a little. Anything anyone needs to surface that we haven't covered?

**Aria:** I have one more. Looker tiles. We have, I think, six hundred tiles. A lot of them are abandoned. Is cleanup part of phase one?

**Priya:** Sort of. We'll inventory them in phase one. We probably won't delete in phase one. Deletion is — politically — usually phase four.

**Aria:** "Politically." (laughs)

**Priya:** Yeah. Deleting someone's dashboard is a way to make an enemy. We will identify the abandoned ones. We will recommend deletion. We will not actually delete without sign-off.

**Aria:** Okay.

**Devansh:** Pricing. I keep meaning to ask. Is the engagement a flat fee or hourly?

**Priya:** Flat fee per phase. We sent the SOW last week — Devansh, you have it. Twelve weeks total, four phases, fixed price per phase. I can resend.

**Devansh:** I have it. I just wanted to confirm in front of Aria.

**Priya:** Cool.

**[09:58]**

**Marcus:** One more architecture thing while we have everyone. Segment. We didn't really talk about Segment.

**Devansh:** Segment is fine. We don't have problems with Segment.

**Marcus:** Famous last words. (laughs) No, I — I just want to make sure that when we do the semantic layer in phase two, we know whether Segment events feed into the same metric definitions or whether they live in their own world.

**Aria:** They live in their own world. Right now. Segment events go into a separate Snowflake schema, EVENTS_RAW, and we don't really model on top of them.

**Marcus:** Okay. So in phase two we have a decision to make about whether to bring them into the canonical layer or keep them separate. Let's make that decision deliberately rather than by accident.

**Aria:** Agreed.

**[10:02]**

**Priya:** Okay. Action items. Let me read them back. Stop me if I get any wrong.

**Priya:** One. Aria provisions read-only access to Looker, dbt Cloud, and Snowflake by end of day today, April twenty-second. Quentin handles the Snowflake role.

**Aria:** Confirmed.

**Quentin:** Confirmed.

**Priya:** Two. I send a draft data-handling addendum to Devansh by Wednesday April twenty-ninth.

**Devansh:** Yes.

**Priya:** Three. First weekly review meeting is Thursday April thirtieth at one PM Eastern. Recurring weekly. I'll send the calendar invite today.

**Devansh:** Got it.

**Priya:** Four. Marcus and I deliver phase one kickoff agenda by Monday April twenty-seventh. So you know what we're walking into in week one.

**Marcus:** I'll draft tomorrow.

**Priya:** Five. Coppertide team — Aria, specifically — please share the SOC 2 auditor's questionnaire if you have it, so I can make sure the addendum aligns. Send by the end of the week, April twenty-fourth.

**Aria:** I'll forward it. It's from Devansh's audit firm, but I have a copy.

**Priya:** Six. Quentin — and this is a small one — please dig up whatever notes you have from the August 2024 Fivetran trial. Specifically the Shopify Plus duplicate-order issue. Even if the notes are short, having something written would help phase three.

**Quentin:** I'll look. I might have a Slack thread. Maybe a Notion page. I'll send what I find by Thursday, April twenty-third.

**Priya:** Seven. We don't make a dbt versus SQLMesh decision today. We revisit during phase one once we've seen the dbt project. Open question, parked.

**Marcus:** Parked.

**Priya:** Did I miss anything?

**Devansh:** I think you got it. Oh — one more. Lina mentioned Hearth and Iron's metrics methodology. Do we want to do anything formal with that?

**Priya:** I'd rather not chase it directly. If we end up with a definition that resembles theirs because it's a good definition, fine. But I don't want to design our taxonomy around what a competitor does, especially based on dashboards that we technically shouldn't have seen.

**Devansh:** Agreed. Strike that.

**[10:08]**

**Aria:** One last thing from me. The marketing analyst we want to hire — her name is — I won't say her name on the call — but the timing of the engagement. Phase two delivers a documented semantic layer in week six, which is roughly mid-June. Could she start mid-June and onboard against the new world rather than the old one?

**Priya:** Yes. That would actually be — that would be ideal. The whole point of phase two is that someone new can look at our work and know what "paid revenue" means without asking you. If she starts mid-June, the documentation will still be a little raw, but it'll be there.

**Aria:** Okay. That's helpful for the offer letter timing.

**Devansh:** Agreed, mid-June start.

**[10:11]**

**Priya:** Okay. Last call for anything before we wrap. Going once.

**Marcus:** I'm good.

**Devansh:** Good.

**Aria:** Good.

**Quentin:** Good.

**Priya:** Great. Thank you all. This was — I'm genuinely energized. I think we have a clear picture and a clear plan. I'll send the access request emails and the calendar invite this afternoon. Marcus, talk tonight to align on phase one prep. Everyone else — first review, Thursday April thirtieth, one PM Eastern.

**Devansh:** Talk soon.

**Marcus:** Bye, all.

**Aria:** Thanks Priya. Thanks Marcus.

**Quentin:** Bye.

**[10:15 — call ends]**

---

## Action Items

| # | Item | Owner | Due |
|---|------|-------|-----|
| 1 | Provision read-only access to Looker, dbt Cloud, Snowflake for Priya and Marcus | Aria (Looker, dbt); Quentin (Snowflake) | EOD 2026-04-22 |
| 2 | Send draft data-handling addendum (covering PII scope, retention, data location) to Devansh | Priya | 2026-04-29 |
| 3 | Send recurring calendar invite for weekly review, Thursdays 1 PM ET | Priya | 2026-04-22 (today) |
| 4 | Draft phase 1 kickoff agenda | Marcus | 2026-04-27 |
| 5 | Forward SOC 2 auditor questionnaire to Priya | Aria | 2026-04-24 |
| 6 | Dig up notes from August 2024 Fivetran trial (Shopify Plus duplicate-order issue) | Quentin | 2026-04-23 |
| 7 | First weekly review meeting | All | 2026-04-30, 1 PM ET |

## Open Questions (parked)

- **dbt vs SQLMesh.** Marcus raised SQLMesh as an option for greenfield semantic-layer work. ## 3. Scope of Services

### 3.1 Engagement Overview

Orbital shall perform the analytics modernization services described in this Section 3 (the "Services") across four (4) sequential phases over a twelve (12) week engagement window. Week 1 begins on April 22, 2026. Week 12 concludes on July 10, 2026.

### 3.2 Phase 1 — Audit (Weeks 1–3, April 22, 2026 through May 8, 2026)

Phase 1 establishes a complete and current view of Coppertide's analytics estate.

**Activities:**

(a) Stack mapping. Orbital will inventory Coppertide's data ingestion sources, transformation tooling, warehouse configuration, semantic and BI layer, orchestration, and observability tooling. The inventory shall identify (i) each system in use, (ii) its owner of record at Coppertide, (iii) data flow dependencies, and (iv) any known operational pain points.

(b) dbt model documentation. Orbital will review the existing dbt project, document each model's purpose and lineage, identify undocumented or orphaned models, and produce a dependency graph suitable for use by Coppertide's data team going forward.

(c) Stakeholder interviews. Orbital will conduct structured interviews with at least one designated representative from Coppertide's marketing, operations, and finance functions, for the purpose of capturing how each function defines and uses Coppertide's core metrics. Lina Costa shall be the marketing representative; Aria Tan shall designate the operations and finance representatives no later than April 24, 2026.

**Deliverables:**

- D1.1 Stack Inventory Document (PDF + source markdown).
- D1.2 dbt Model Documentation, including dependency graph (committed to Coppertide's `analytics-platform` repository).
- D1.3 Definitions Interview Readout (PDF), summarizing per-function metric definitions and identifying conflicts to be resolved in Phase 2.

### 3.3 Phase 2 — Foundation (Weeks 4–6, May 11, 2026 through May 29, 2026)

Phase 2 establishes Coppertide's canonical semantic layer.

**Activities:**

(a) Canonical metric definitions. Orbital will produce signed-off definitions for each of the five (5) core metrics: gross revenue, net revenue, active customer, repeat customer, and marketing-attributed revenue. Each definition shall include (i) the natural-language definition, (ii) the SQL implementation, (iii) the time-grain semantics, (iv) the underlying source tables, and (v) the named owner at Coppertide.

(b) Semantic layer implementation. Orbital will implement the canonical metrics as a dbt semantic layer, organized in a new `models/semantic/` namespace, with associated tests and exposures.

(c) Pilot dashboards. Orbital will produce two (2) pilot dashboards in Coppertide's existing BI tool, each consuming exclusively from the new semantic layer. The first dashboard shall be a Marketing Performance dashboard owned by Lina Costa; the second shall be an Executive Weekly Review dashboard owned by Devansh Mehta.

**Deliverables:**

- D2.1 dbt Semantic Layer Pull Request, opened against `main` of Coppertide's `analytics-platform` repository, with reviewers Aria Tan and Quentin Reyes.
- D2.2 Metrics Definitions Document (PDF + source markdown), countersigned by Aria Tan and Devansh Mehta.
- D2.3 Two pilot dashboards, deployed to production and accessible to their respective owners.

### 3.4 Phase 3 — Migration Evaluation (Weeks 7–9, June 1, 2026 through June 19, 2026)

Phase 3 produces a defensible recommendation regarding Coppertide's long-term ingestion architecture.

**Activities:**

(a) Trial implementations. Orbital will stand up a time-boxed Fivetran trial covering an agreed subset of Coppertide's source systems (the "Trial Sources"), and, in parallel, a custom Postgres CDC pipeline covering the same Trial Sources. The Trial Sources shall be agreed in writing between the Parties no later than June 1, 2026, and shall include at minimum: the Postgres operational database, the Shopify storefront feed, and the warehouse-management system at Coppertide's Reno facility.

(b) Side-by-side benchmarks. Orbital will benchmark the two trial implementations on the following dimensions: (i) total cost of ownership at Coppertide's projected 12-month volume, (ii) end-to-end latency, (iii) operational burden (paging frequency, schema-change handling, observability), (iv) vendor and key-personnel risk, and (v) extensibility to additional source systems.

(c) Recommendation. Orbital will produce a written recommendation of one of the two architectures, with explicit reasoning tied to the benchmark results and to Coppertide's stated constraints.

**Deliverables:**

- D3.1 Fivetran vs. Postgres CDC Benchmark Report (PDF + source markdown), including raw measurements and methodology.
- D3.2 Recommendation Memo (PDF), addressed to Devansh Mehta and Aria Tan, of no fewer than three (3) and no more than eight (8) pages.

### 3.5 Phase 4 — Handoff (Weeks 10–12, June 22, 2026 through July 10, 2026)

Phase 4 transfers operational ownership of all engagement work product to Coppertide's in-house data team.

**Activities:**

(a) Runbooks. Orbital will produce written runbooks for each of the systems, models, and pipelines delivered or materially modified during the engagement, in a format suitable for use by Coppertide's on-call rotation.

(b) Training sessions. Orbital will deliver two (2) live training sessions, each of approximately ninety (90) minutes, recorded for future reference. The first session shall cover the dbt semantic layer and metric ownership model and shall be led by Priya Iyer. The second session shall cover the recommended ingestion architecture and its operational profile and shall be led by Marcus Lehrer. Quentin Reyes and Aria Tan shall be the primary attendees; additional attendees may be invited at Coppertide's discretion.

(c) Final playbook. Orbital will produce a Post-Engagement Playbook documenting (i) the state of the analytics estate as of engagement close, (ii) the recommended sequence of work for the following two (2) quarters, and (iii) decisions deferred during the engagement that Coppertide should revisit.

(d) Post-engagement support window. For thirty (30) calendar days following the engagement end date, Orbital shall provide reasonable email support to Quentin Reyes and Aria Tan, on a best-efforts basis, regarding the deliverables produced under this SoW. The support window does not include net-new development, on-call coverage, or guaranteed response-time service levels. Targeted total support effort during the window is up to twelve (12) hours of Orbital's time.

**Deliverables:**

- D4.1 Runbooks (markdown, committed to Coppertide's `analytics-platform/docs/runbooks/` directory).
- D4.2 Two training sessions delivered live, with recordings provided to Coppertide.
- D4.3 Final Post-Engagement Playbook (PDF + source markdown).
- D4.4 Thirty-day post-engagement support window, ending August 9, 2026.

### 3.6 Out of Scope

The following are expressly out of scope for this engagement and shall not be undertaken by Orbital absent a written change order:

(a) Migration of any production data ingestion pipeline from one architecture to another (Phase 3 is evaluation only; the migration itself, if approved by Coppertide, is a separate engagement).

(b) Any changes to Coppertide's BI tool licensing, identity provider configuration, or network security posture.

(c) Implementation of customer-facing analytics features, embedded analytics, or any work whose primary consumer is a Coppertide end customer rather than a Coppertide employee.

(d) Engineering or data work pertaining to systems located physically at the Reno warehouse, other than read-only access to the warehouse-management system feed.

(e) Compliance, audit, or regulatory work (including but not limited to PCI, SOC 2, and HIPAA scope work).

## 2. What I think is actually going on at Coppertide

The SoW phrases the problem as a tooling problem — Stitch is expensive ($2,034/mo in April, hitting row-volume limits at ~14M Klaviyo events/day after the Spring Pans campaign), Snowflake is $800/mo and idle, Looker is $1,400/mo for four creator seats and nobody can agree on what "revenue" means in any dashboard. That framing is convenient because it points at line items on a SaaS bill, which is a thing Devansh's CFO can react to.

It is not the actual problem.

Here is what I heard underneath the kickoff call, and Marcus, push back on this if you read it differently:

**The real bottleneck is metric definitional drift, not tooling.** Aria has been firefighting reconciliation between Looker dashboards, Shopify reports, and the weekly exec deck for at least the last two quarters — she said "I spend Mondays explaining why two numbers don't match" almost verbatim. That is not a Stitch problem. That is a problem where there are at least three definitions of "net revenue" floating around — Shopify gross, Shopify minus refunds, Shopify minus refunds minus marketing-attributed discounts — and nobody owns the canonical one. If we replace Stitch with Fivetran tomorrow and don't touch the semantic layer, Aria still spends Mondays the same way. She just has a cheaper data pipeline carrying ambiguous numbers faster.

**Devansh's "ingestion ownership" line is about audit, not about cost.** Watch what he said carefully: "I want PII to stay in US infrastructure" and "the SOC 2 thing." He did not say "I want to save money on Stitch." He said the cost number, but the urgency is compliance. That changes how we evaluate Phase 3. A self-hosted CDC option (Debezium on their own infra, or a managed Fivetran with HVR-style on-prem agents) becomes more attractive than a pure SaaS Fivetran for reasons that have nothing to do with the engineering merits. We need to be honest with him about that — the "best technical choice" and the "best compliance choice" might be different rows in our matrix and he has to pick. Not us.

**The Looker situation is a governance problem dressed up as a license problem.** Four creator seats at Coppertide means four people each maintaining their own LookML, drifting from each other. Lina's marketing dashboards don't reconcile to Aria's finance views because they are literally different models pointing at different (but adjacent) tables. Cutting seats fixes the bill, not the governance. The semantic layer in dbt is where this gets fixed, and it gets fixed by us writing the metric definitions down — in version-controlled YAML — and getting Aria to bless them. That is a stakeholder-management problem, not a coding problem, and it's why I want Phase 1 to be Priya-heavy.

**Quentin is the bus factor.** He has been the sole data eng for ~18 months. Devansh said it casually but I clocked it: "Quentin built most of the Stitch integrations." If Quentin leaves before our handoff (Phase 4), our documentation has to be airtight or this entire $120k engagement evaporates into one person's tribal knowledge. He also seemed exhausted on the call. I want to take him seriously as a stakeholder, not just as a junior engineer who'll execute what we design.

**They tried Fivetran in 2024 and got burned by the Shopify Plus duplicate-orders bug.** That bug is fixed (Fivetran shipped the connector rewrite in late Q3 2024) but the institutional memory is "Fivetran broke us." We need to address this directly in Phase 3 with documentation, not hand-wave it. If we recommend Fivetran and don't surface the 2024 incident in our writeup, Devansh will not trust us on the next decision.

**The Klaviyo 14M events/day number is a Spring Pans peak, not a steady-state.** Spring Pans was a campaign, not a baseline. If we size Phase 3 ingestion economics on the peak number, we'll oversize the recommendation. I want Marcus to pull at least 90 days of Stitch row-volume telemetry in W1 — actual daily counts, not what Coppertide told us — and let's size against the P75, not the peak.

# Coppertide — Company Overview

_Working dossier. Mix of public-source research and notes captured during the kickoff call on 2026-04-22. Not an SoW, not a pitch; this is the version of Coppertide I want in my head before every working session with them._

---

## 1. At a glance

Coppertide is a direct-to-consumer cookware brand founded in 2019, headquartered in SoHo, New York City, with warehousing and fulfillment out of Reno, Nevada. They sell copper-core stainless cookware — not copper-veneer, the distinction matters to them — manufactured in Portugal and sold primarily through coppertide.com. They closed a $32M Series B in Q3 2025 led by Forerunner Ventures, are at roughly $40M ARR with ~35% YoY growth, and employ around 80 people. The company is in the middle of its biggest paid marketing campaign ever ("Spring Pans," April 2026) and the data-stack strain from that campaign is what brought us in.

---

## 2. Origin and product

### Founders and founding story

- **Maya Rosenfeld** — CEO, co-founder. Previously growth lead at Allbirds. The NYT Style profile (Aug 2024) framed the founding story as Maya being frustrated that "good cookware looked like restaurant equipment and bad cookware looked like a Pinterest board," and wanting a third lane. She is the public face of the brand and does most of the founder-led press.
- **Hugo Vasquez** — Chief Product Officer, co-founder. Industrial designer by training, spent the years before Coppertide at Snow Peak in Japan working on outdoor cooking gear. Hugo is the reason the product line is small and considered; in the NYT piece Maya credits him with the "no SKU before its time" rule that has kept the catalog tight.

The two met through a mutual friend in 2018 and spent roughly a year prototyping before launching the first Daily Pan in late 2019. The brand quietly grew through 2020-2021 on word of mouth and a few well-placed gift guides; the inflection point was the move from a small US contract manufacturer to Casa Ferreira Metals in Portugal in 2021, which let them stabilize quality and unit economics simultaneously.

### Product lineup

- **The Daily Pan** — 10-inch sauté pan. Hero SKU. Drives roughly half of unit volume (inferred from Devansh's offhand mention on the kickoff that "if Daily Pan stops moving we feel it the same day").
- **The Sunday Pot** — 5-quart Dutch oven. Higher AOV, gift-driven seasonality.
- **2-piece skillet bundle** — entry-into-the-system SKU; bundle pricing softens the first-purchase ask.
- Price band across the line: $145–$340. They have deliberately not gone below $145; in the Modern Retail interview Devansh said the floor is "a brand decision Maya owns, not a margin decision."

### Manufacturing

- **Casa Ferreira Metals** in Portugal manufactures the entire line under contract since 2021.
- Coppertide retains design, materials specification, and quality control. There is a small QC team that travels to Portugal on a quarterly cadence (mentioned by Hugo in a Lenny's Newsletter side-comment, repeated on a Maya podcast appearance).
- The "made in Portugal" narrative is load-bearing for the brand, distinct from competitors who manufacture in China or Italy.

---

## 3. Funding and growth

- **Series B closed Q3 2025**, $32M raised, led by Forerunner Ventures. Reuters ran a short on the announcement (Reuters, Sept 2025); the press release leaned heavily on the "DTC + selective wholesale" thesis.
- **Eurie Kim** (Forerunner partner) sits on the board and attends board meetings — surfaced in passing during the kickoff call when Devansh referenced a "board push" on attribution clarity.
- **Reported ARR: ~$40M**, growth ~35% YoY. These were the numbers Maya cited in the NYT profile and reaffirmed in the Series B announcement; consistent across both, no reason to discount.
- Prior rounds (inferred from public coverage, not confirmed by us): a seed and Series A that pre-date Forerunner. We don't have firm sizes and shouldn't quote any.

The growth shape worth noting: 35% YoY at $40M is healthy but not blistering for a Series B at a Forerunner-led valuation — meaning the board is likely watching efficiency metrics (CAC payback, contribution margin) more than top-line. This colors the marketing-finance friction described later.

---

## 4. Leadership and team

- **Maya Rosenfeld** — CEO. Public-facing, brand-driven, growth-marketing background. Approves the floor on price points; owns brand voice.
- **Hugo Vasquez** — CPO and co-founder. Product, materials, and the manufacturing relationship with Casa Ferreira. Less public; rarely on podcasts.
- **Devansh Mehta** — CTO, hired 2023. Came from Wayfair's data platform org. Public LinkedIn signals a strong data-engineering bias for a CTO at this size; the Modern Retail interview made it clear he reasons in build-vs-buy frames and is comfortable saying out loud when a vendor is past its useful life. He is our primary day-to-day counterpart.
- **Lina Costa** — VP Marketing, hired 2024 from Outdoor Voices. Owns paid, brand, and lifecycle. Mentioned admiring **Hearth & Iron** (a smaller competitor) during the kickoff — useful tell about how she thinks about positioning.
- **Aria Tan** — Head of Analytics, hired early 2025 from Glossier. Reports into Devansh, not Lina, which is itself an interesting choice and tells you something about how this org wants analytics to work (technical-first, not marketing-first).
- **Sebastian Park** — CFO, hired late 2025. The newest senior hire. Raised the "paid revenue" definition friction with the board in the Q4 2025 board meeting (per Devansh on the kickoff). Worth assuming he is still establishing his standing internally and will be sensitive to anything that lets him land a clean win on financial reporting.

### Engineering team detail

- 12 engineers total under Devansh.
- **Quentin Reyes** — sole data engineer, 7 months in. Came in via a referral from Aria's prior team at Glossier (kickoff call, 2026-04-22). The fact that the data engineer was an Aria-network hire and not a Devansh-network hire is a subtle org signal: analytics drove the hire even though the role reports up through engineering. Quentin will be our hands-on partner; everything we ship needs to be operable by one person.

---

## 5. Channels and operations

### Channel mix

- **80% direct** via coppertide.com (Shopify Plus). Where the brand wants to live and where most of the data lives clean.
- **15% wholesale**, almost entirely **Williams-Sonoma**, started late 2024. Lina has flagged internally that the numbers are "mixed" (kickoff call) — not yet a public concern but a clear undertow.
- **5% Amazon**, deliberately small. Maya has spoken publicly (NYT, podcast appearances) about Amazon as a defensive presence rather than a growth channel — they're there so counterfeiters can't squat the listing.

### Wholesale pause

In a January 2026 CEO blog post, Maya announced a pause on adding new wholesale partners through Q1 2026: "We will not add new wholesale partners this quarter; we want our DTC engine running clean before we layer more." That blog post is, in retrospect, a leading indicator of the project we're now engaged on — they decided in January that the DTC stack needed to be in order before the company widened its retail footprint.

### Operations

- **HQ in SoHo, NYC.** Hybrid in-office on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday; remote-flexible Monday and Friday. (Confirmed kickoff call.)
- **Warehouse and fulfillment in Reno, Nevada** since 2022. The move from a 3PL to in-house Reno fulfillment is one of the under-told operational stories — not a press moment, but referenced obliquely in the Modern Retail interview as "the year we stopped being surprised by our own inventory numbers."
- **Quarterly off-sites.** Next one is **Hudson Valley, May 19–21, 2026**; Devansh and Aria will both be off the call schedule that week. We need to plan around that — it's right in the middle of a likely first delivery window.

---

## 6. Engineering and data stack

This is the section that matters most for how we engage. Sources are a mix of Devansh's LinkedIn, the Modern Retail podcast (Feb 2025), and what was confirmed live on the kickoff call (2026-04-22).

### Application stack

- **Shopify Plus** for the storefront. Standard for DTC at this revenue band; almost certainly the source of truth for orders.
- **Custom Node.js middleware.** Sits between Shopify, the warehouse system, and downstream systems. Devansh's LinkedIn lists "Node.js services orchestrating Shopify webhooks" — consistent with what was discussed on the call.
- **Postgres on RDS** as the operational database backing the middleware.
- **Datadog** for observability (per Devansh's LinkedIn). Not sure how deeply instrumented; safe assumption is "infra metrics, decent; application traces, partial."

### Data stack

- **Stitch** for ingestion, current April invoice **$2,034/mo**. Per the Modern Retail podcast (Feb 2025), Devansh said they were "still on Stitch but it won't last another year." That was a forecast 14 months ago; the Spring Pans Klaviyo event volume has now made it operational, not strategic, that they replace it. This is the wedge.
- **Snowflake** as the warehouse, currently under-utilized at roughly **$800/mo**. The under-utilization is itself a signal — they have headroom to absorb properly-modeled data without an immediate compute conversation.
- **dbt Cloud** for transformations. **One project, two production models, undocumented.** This is the part of the stack that Aria almost certainly wants to grow but cannot grow yet because the upstream is broken. Useful to keep in mind: any improvement here that Aria can take credit for is welcome, but it's not the project we were hired for.
- **Looker** for BI. **$1,400/mo, four creator seats.** Four creators at a company of 80 is a specific choice — they want a small group to own the model layer rather than letting dashboards proliferate. Consistent with Aria's Glossier background.
- **Segment** for events. The Klaviyo events flowing through Segment are the proximate cause of the Stitch strain.

### What's missing or weak (inferred)

- **No catalog/lineage tooling.** Not surprising at this size, but combined with two undocumented dbt models, the institutional knowledge of "what does this column actually mean" lives in Quentin's head and partly in Aria's.
- **No reverse ETL.** I haven't seen one mentioned; given the marketing-finance friction described below, this is going to come up eventually.
- **Probably no formal data SLAs.** Inferred from the conversation tone — when asked about freshness expectations on the kickoff, Devansh's answer was "morning numbers should look like yesterday," which is a real expectation but not a contractually expressed one.

---

## 7. Compliance and security posture

- **SOC 2 in progress, target completion Q3 2026.** This is the source of Devansh's "PII stays in US" requirement (kickoff call).
- The PII-stays-in-US rule constrains vendor selection on anything new we recommend. Any tool with EU-only or EU-default data residency is a non-starter without a US-region option.
- Data classification (inferred): customer PII (name, address, email, phone), order data (PCI-adjacent but Shopify holds the card data, so they're out of scope for the heavy PCI lift), and event data through Segment that may carry identifiers.
- The Series B raised the bar on security expectations from the board; SOC 2 is a board-tracked deliverable, not just a sales-enablement one (inferred from the timing — SOC 2 push starting after Series B close is a common pattern).

---

## 8. Competitive context

The cookware DTC space has gotten crowded. Coppertide's named competitors and how I read each:

- **Made In** — the most visible direct competitor. Larger, broader catalog, more wholesale-forward. Coppertide's copper-core narrative is a deliberate counter to Made In's "professional-grade" positioning.
- **Caraway** — design-led, ceramic-coated, lower price band. Different customer at the margin, but they show up in the same gift guides. Coppertide doesn't pretend to compete on price.
- **Great Jones** — closer to Coppertide in tone (smaller catalog, founder-driven brand, design press). Has had its own well-publicized turbulence; Coppertide rarely names them but they're in the comparable set.
- **Hearth & Iron** — smaller, design-forward, mentioned approvingly by Lina on the kickoff call. The fact that Lina spontaneously named a smaller competitor she admires is more useful than the named-large-competitor list — it tells me where she thinks the brand should aspire on aesthetics.

### Coppertide's stated differentiation

- **Copper core, not copper veneer.** They will correct interviewers on this.
- **Lifetime warranty.** A capital-allocation choice as much as a marketing one; affects how they think about return rates and durability data.
- **Made in Portugal.** Tied to the Casa Ferreira relationship; the narrative depends on that partnership staying intact (see risks below).

---

## 9. Recent press and public moments

- **NYT Style profile of Maya, August 2024** — "How a former growth marketer made copper cookware cool again." Brand and product focused. The piece is the canonical version of the Coppertide origin story; if you read one external source on the company, read this one. (NYT Style, Aug 2024)
- **Modern Retail podcast with Devansh, February 2025** — Devansh on build-vs-buy for the data stack; the explicit "Stitch won't last another year" line is from this episode. He also discussed Snowflake as a multi-year bet and was vague-on-purpose about dbt's role. (Modern Retail podcast, Feb 2025)
- **Reuters short on the Series B, September 2025** — Standard funding-announcement copy; useful for the Forerunner-led detail and the $32M figure. (Reuters, Sept 2025)
- **Maya on Lenny's Newsletter, January 2026** — Mentioned the Casa Ferreira labor dispute in passing, framed as resolved. Also where the "Q1 wholesale pause" thinking was previewed before the formal blog post. (Lenny's Newsletter, Jan 2026)
- **CEO blog post, January 2026** — Formal announcement of the wholesale pause through Q1 2026. (Coppertide blog, Jan 2026)
- **Spring Pans campaign, April 2026** — Biggest paid spend in company history. Drove the Klaviyo event volume spike now overwhelming Stitch. Not a press moment per se, but a public commercial moment with internal data-system consequences. (Coppertide marketing, April 2026)

---

## 10. Cultural notes and operational rhythms

For engagement scheduling and how to read the room.

### Rhythms

- **Hybrid Tue/Wed/Thu in-office.** Default sync windows for us should land in those days. Mondays and Fridays are remote-friendly but lighter on cross-functional decisions.
- **Quarterly off-sites.** Next: Hudson Valley, May 19–21, 2026. Devansh and Aria off the call schedule that week (kickoff call, 2026-04-22). Plan delivery milestones around it.
- **Weekly engineering standup**, Tuesday mornings (inferred from the way Devansh referenced "Tuesday standup" without explanation).
- **Board meetings quarterly**, with Eurie Kim from Forerunner attending.

### Cultural reads

- **Small, considered catalog culture.** Hugo's "no SKU before its time" rule extends beyond product into how the org makes other decisions; they prefer fewer things done well. This is consistent with the under-utilized Snowflake and the four-seat Looker — they don't add tooling for tooling's sake.
- **Analytics-respected.** Aria reports up through engineering, has a Glossier pedigree, and was given a sole-headcount data engineer hire within months of joining. The org takes analytics seriously even if the current state is messy.
- **Marketing-finance tension at the executive level.** The "paid revenue" definition disagreement that Sebastian raised in the Q4 2025 board meeting has not been resolved (kickoff call). It has been a board-level topic for two quarters running, which means it's now structural, not interpersonal. Any work we do that touches attribution, paid metrics, or revenue definitions will be politically loaded.
- **Founder-led press, professionalized internals.** Maya and Hugo do the public storytelling; Devansh, Lina, Aria, and Sebastian run the company. Coppertide is past the stage where the founders are in the operational details day-to-day.

### Communication style

- Devansh is precise, uses build-vs-buy framings, comfortable saying things out loud that other CTOs would hedge. Match his register; don't over-soften.
- Lina is brand-fluent and references peer brands by name. Worth doing the brand reading before any conversation she's in.
- Aria has not been in much public material yet; on the kickoff call she was quieter but asked the sharpest single question (about how we handle backfills without breaking lineage). Treat her input as load-bearing even when it's brief.

---

## 11. Open risks and sensitivities

Things to track week-over-week, in roughly the order I'd worry about them.

### Active operational risk

- **Spring Pans Klaviyo spike.** Ongoing. Stitch is the choke point. Anything we recommend has to be designable around live traffic — we cannot do a clean cutover during the campaign. Inferred: the campaign tail will run at least into early May, possibly later if it's working.

Priya's primary point of contact is **Aria Tan (Head of Analytics)**. Technical sponsor is **Devansh Mehta (CTO)**. Aria is responsive and trusts Priya; Devansh is more skeptical and will be the harder of the two to keep aligned.

  - Phase 1 (weeks 1–3): warehouse + ingestion stand-up. Snowflake, Fivetran connectors for Shopify, Klaviyo, NetSuite, and the Coppertide application Postgres.
  - Phase 2 (weeks 4–7): staging and intermediate dbt models. This is where Priya does most of the modeling work.
  - Phase 3 (weeks 8–12): marts, semantic layer (Looker), reference dashboards, knowledge transfer.

- **Aubergine Finance (fintech, prior client).** Engagement wrapped two months ago (late February 2026). Successful — they delivered against the original scope and a small Phase 2. Post-engagement reference call is **scheduled for 2026-05-08**. Reference contact is **Vivek Sundaresan (CTO)**, with whom Priya has a good rapport. The reference call is primarily for two prospect introductions Vivek has offered to make.

### Open question with Marcus

They are discussing whether Orbital should take on a second client for the second half of 2026 (a hypothetical engagement starting around July). Marcus's position is yes — Orbital has the bandwidth and a healthy pipeline. Priya's position is hesitant: she does not want to commit to a second client until Coppertide's Phase 3 lands cleanly, because Phase 3 is where the $69k overrun risk concentrates. She is not closed on it; she wants to revisit after week 8 of Coppertide. Marcus has agreed to that timeline informally but has been quietly seeding pipeline conversations anyway.

### Upcoming commitments

- **2026-04-28 (Tuesday) — dental appointment.** Will affect Tuesday morning availability that week. She has already moved her usual Tuesday client check-in to Wednesday morning.
- **Mid-May (likely 2026-05-13 or 2026-05-14) — PyData Bangalore talk.** Title: "dbt at startup scale". Slides are roughly 60% done. The talk is in person; she has done the room before. She is mildly stressed about the timing because Coppertide Phase 1 wraps the same week.
- **2026-05-08 (Friday) — Aubergine Finance reference call** with Vivek Sundaresan.
- **Weekly Coppertide standup** — Monday/Wednesday/Friday, 7:30 PM IST. This is the recurring cadence she negotiated with Aria.

### Risks she's actively tracking

1. Coppertide Phase 3 overrun ($69k internal; the engagement is fixed-price so this is Orbital's exposure, not the client's).
2. Devansh Mehta as a technical-sponsor risk: he prefers SQLMesh and has already asked twice why Orbital is using dbt. Priya is going to write a one-page rationale doc this week.
3. The PyData talk colliding with Coppertide Phase 1 wrap.
4. A small risk that Marcus moves ahead with a second-half-2026 client before Phase 3 of Coppertide is locked in.

### Personal calendar (next two weeks)

- **2026-04-28 (Tue):** dental appointment, morning.
- **2026-05-02 (Sat):** Devika visiting Bangalore for the weekend.
- **2026-05-08 (Fri):** Aubergine reference call (work, but on her personal cal because it's pre-9-AM-IST as a US-East call).
- **2026-05-13 / 2026-05-14:** PyData Bangalore (one of these two days, depending on final schedule).

## Working-style preferences

These are firm. They are not aspirations.

- **No meetings before 9 AM IST.** Mornings are for deep work — modeling, writing, code. She will turn down a 7 AM call from a US client unless it is a contractual escalation. (Late-evening calls are her US-East slot, not early-morning.)
- **Deep-work blocks are 90 minutes.** She books them on her calendar in 90-minute units. Slack is closed during these blocks. She does not accept calls during them. If a client tries to reschedule into one, she pushes back.
- **Async over sync above 30 minutes.** If a topic is going to need more than half an hour, her default is to ask for a written brief instead of a meeting. Most Coppertide work is structured this way.
- **Two-call-a-day cap.** She tries (not always successfully) to keep synchronous calls to two per day. More than that and she finds the modeling work slips.
- **No working on Saturdays.** Sundays are negotiable for prep work; Saturdays are not.

## Notable opinions and stances

These are positions she has held publicly enough that they are worth recording as part of her profile.

- **Stitch is a low-quality vendor.** She has run into reliability and connector-coverage problems with Stitch on two past engagements (one at Square, one early at Orbital). She will not recommend Stitch to a new client. If a prospective client is currently on Stitch, she will recommend a migration to Fivetran (or, in compliance-bound cases, custom Postgres CDC) as part of any engagement she takes.
- **dbt vs SQLMesh.** This is the live disagreement with Marcus. Marcus prefers SQLMesh for greenfield engagements, citing the virtual environments / column-level lineage / migration story. Priya's view is that for most Orbital clients, the switching cost from dbt is not worth it — clients have invested in dbt training, dbt's ecosystem (packages, CI tooling, hiring pool) is broader, and SQLMesh's advantages are more theoretical than practical for the kinds of warehouses Orbital builds. Her position is not "SQLMesh is bad" — it's "the marginal benefit doesn't beat the switching cost for our clients." She and Marcus have agreed to disagree; greenfield Orbital projects are dbt by default unless a specific client wants otherwise.
- **A dbt model without `description:` and tests is a failed deliverable.** This is a hard rule on her engagements. Every model that ships must have (a) a `description:` in the YAML, (b) at least one test (uniqueness on a primary key counts as the minimum bar), and (c) column-level descriptions for any column that a downstream BI user would touch. She will not sign off on a milestone that violates this rule. She has, in past engagements, pushed milestones by a week to get this right.
- **BI tool selection scales with team size.** Looker for clients under ~50 employees who need a single source of truth. Mode / Hex for analytics-heavy SaaS where SQL-native exploration matters more than governance. Tableau is rarely her recommendation — she finds the modeling layer too thin and the licensing too painful.
- **Ingestion: managed by default.** Fivetran for most clients. Custom Postgres CDC only when there is a real compliance reason (HIPAA, certain financial-data residency situations). She actively pushes back on "let's build our own connectors" conversations.
- **Real-time is usually overkill.** Her default reaction to "we need real-time data" is to ask what decision is being made. In her experience, 90% of stated real-time requirements are actually "hourly is fine, but the dashboard needs to feel responsive."
- **Snowflake over BigQuery for new clients.** Predictable cost surface, decent governance, less surprise. Not a religious position — she will run BigQuery if the client is already on GCP — but she does not recommend a switch from one to the other.

## Public presence

Priya has a small, deliberate public footprint. She is not active on social media beyond LinkedIn and a sparingly-used Twitter account. She does not write a blog. Her public surface is mostly conference talks and the occasional podcast.

- **Coalesce 2024 — panelist.** She was on a panel titled "Data engineering for non-data-engineering companies." The panel was well attended (she remembers it as her first time on a stage that big) and is the talk she most often references when introducing herself in client calls. She did not give a solo talk at Coalesce 2024 — only the panel.
- **PyData Bangalore — upcoming, mid-May 2026.** Title: "dbt at startup scale." Solo talk, ~30 minutes. Slides are 60% done as of 2026-04-22. The talk argues for a specific project layout for early-stage dbt projects, drawn from her experience at Orbital. This will be her first solo talk in India.
- **Podcast appearances.** She has been on two industry podcasts (one in 2023, one in 2025), both in the data-engineering niche. She does not seek these out but says yes when asked.
- **LinkedIn.** Updated. Posts maybe once a month. No newsletter.
- **Twitter / X.** Account exists. Mostly retweets. She does not post hot takes.
- **GitHub.** Active under the Orbital org; her personal account has been quiet since 2023. She contributes occasionally to one mid-sized dbt package but is not a maintainer.

## Notes on this profile

- Reference date: 2026-04-22.
- Tone is intentionally factual rather than promotional. This is a memory document, not a bio.
- The Recent Context section is the part that will go stale fastest; expect to revise after Coppertide Phase 1 lands (week of 2026-05-13).
