After two weeks, you can start gardening again gently — pulling weeds is fine, hauling bags of soil is not yet. The stained-glass kiln will have to wait until Dr. Park clears you at your follow-up visit.

You have a small bottle of **nitroglycerin tablets** to keep with you. If you ever get chest pain or that pressure feeling again, sit down, put one tablet under your tongue, and let it dissolve. Wait 5 minutes. If the pain isn't gone, take a second tablet. Wait 5 more minutes. If still no relief, take a third — and if that still doesn't fix it, **call 911**. Do not drive yourself.

### New Medications — Counseling

**Clopidogrel 75 mg PO daily.** Indication: stent thrombosis prevention as the thienopyridine partner to aspirin in the post-PCI DAPT regimen. Rationale for the swap: ticagrelor, while preferred in many post-ACS protocols, carries a higher numerical bleeding-risk signal than clopidogrel in head-to-head comparative datasets; given the patient's confirmed UGI bleed event 12 days post-PCI on ticagrelor, switching the thienopyridine partner is indicated. No loading dose is required because aspirin has been continuous and the stent is already 12 days old; steady-state platelet inhibition with clopidogrel will be achieved within several days. **The patient asked, "Is clopidogrel as protective as ticagrelor for my stent?"** This was explicitly answered: in his specific scenario — post-PCI, on stable DAPT with continuous aspirin, recovering from a confirmed bleed — clopidogrel is the preferred replacement, and the available data support adequate stent protection at this stage with aspirin 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg. He was advised to **never** stop either antiplatelet without explicit cardiology approval.

**Drug-interaction note (acknowledged in EHR):** the prescription system flagged a clopidogrel-omeprazole interaction alert; this alert was **acknowledged and resolved by selecting pantoprazole as the PPI of choice**, which does not meaningfully inhibit CYP2C19 and is the recommended PPI partner for clopidogrel.

Will be reassessed at 8 weeks (target reassessment week of 2026-01-19) — the patient asked, **"Will I have to take pantoprazole forever?"** and was answered: no — 8 weeks then reassess; long-term low-dose PPI may be considered going forward only if specific risk factors persist. ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — PRIVILEGED. Park v. Karras Custom Builders LLC — Initial Case Strategy. Author: Carmen Ostrowski. Date: 2026-02-13. Matter OL-2026-0019.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Kitchen-renovation breach-of-contract case with strong consumer-protection overlays. Wendell Park retained Ostrowski Legal 2026-02-11 after Karras Custom Builders LLC walked off the job 2026-01-22 over a disputed $4,500 change-order invoice never reduced to writing. Wendell paid $18,000 against a $24,500 contract signed 2025-11-04; we have an independent repair estimate from Aldous Bremer (Bremer & Sons) dated 2026-02-12 of $14,200 to remediate five defects: off-level cabinets, cracked quartz seam, loose tile and grout, a non-GFCI outlet within six feet of the sink, and a range hood vented into a cabinet rather than the exterior. The legal theory is over-determined — common-law breach, implied warranty, NY GBL §349, NYC HIC violations, code-based statutory hooks — but the practical question is forum and timing, not liability.

Recommendation, ratified by Wendell at the 02-11 retainer signing with article-by-article initialing: file in Kings County Civil Court — Small Claims Part and claim $7,500, deliberately at-or-near the $10,000 cap. Plausibly provable damages ($14,200 cost of cure plus consequentials) exceed the cap; election waives recovery of the excess in this forum. We accept the waiver for (a) a hearing ~six weeks out rather than 12+ months, (b) a flat $1,500 fee the case can support, (c) Wendell's preference for a fast, contained resolution, and (d) denial to Karras of the jury demand he would otherwise make. Settlement window is real but not yet ripe; opposing counsel will not retain until the complaint is filed. Mail demand 2026-02-19, file 2026-02-26 if no substantive response, first hearing Friday 2026-03-20, 9:30 AM, Part 5, before Hon. Marisol Vega.

## 2. Facts (succinct)

Contract 2025-11-04, signed by Wendell Park and Stefan Karras for $24,500 to renovate the kitchen at 1612 Argyle Road, Ditmas Park. Scope: custom shaker-style maple cabinets, quartz countertops, porcelain floor tile, electrical updates including code-mandated GFCI outlets near the sink. Start 2025-12-01; promised completion 2026-01-15. Payment: $8,000 deposit (paid 2025-11-04), $8,000 mid-project (paid 2025-12-22), $8,500 on completion. Wendell paid $18,000 total; he refused the $4,500 change-order invoice Karras issued 2026-01-15 because it was not in writing and reflected work he never approved at that price. Karras walked off 2026-01-22 after the kitchen argument over that invoice, leaving five defects: cabinets off-level by 1/2 inch on the south wall run; quartz cracked along the seam within three weeks of install (visible by 2026-01-08); ~six floor tiles loose with grout cracking in two areas; outlet adjacent to the sink not GFCI; range hood terminating inside the upper cabinet rather than the exterior. Bremer's 2026-02-12 written estimate to remediate all five: $14,200 on Bremer & Sons letterhead, shop at 4128 18th Avenue, Brooklyn.

## 3. Legal Theories

**Theory 1 — Common-law breach of contract.** Services-dominant contract; the predominant-purpose test takes us out of UCC Article 2 even though goods (cabinets, quartz, tile) pass through. We plead a valid written contract, performance by Wendell to $18,000, material breach by Karras through defective work on five items and abandonment 2026-01-22, and damages measured by cost of cure ($14,200) less unpaid balance ($6,500). Cost-of-cure is the right measure because defects are repairable rather than going to fundamental purpose; the $7,500 claim is well-supported even after the cap.

**Theory 2 — NYC HIC violations, NYC Admin Code §20-393 et seq.** Karras holds NYC HIC license #1374829, but his contract terms and post-walk-off conduct may violate the HIC chapter, particularly around written change-order requirements and scope. Renee is pulling the DCWP record this week to verify the license was active throughout the job. An active license does not insulate against §20-393 substantive violations.

**Theory 3 — NY GBL §349 deceptive acts in consumer transactions.** Consumer suit by any measure: a homeowner hiring a residential contractor for a primary residence. The hook is the representation that work was completed to code (range hood; GFCI) when it was not, and a $4,500 change-order invoice whose alleged authorization fails GBL §771's writing requirement. §349 carries actual damages, possible treble up to $1,000, and attorney's fees — fee-shifting is meaningful even in small-claims because it can underwrite the flat fee on the back end.

**Theory 4 — NYC Electrical Code violation.** NEC 210.8(A)(7) requires GFCI protection for receptacles within six feet of the outside edge of a sink; the NYC Electrical Code incorporates the NEC by reference. The non-GFCI outlet adjacent to Wendell's sink is a facial code violation — a damages anchor, evidence of bad workmanship under Theory 1, and a deceptive representation under Theory 3.

**Theory 5 — Implied warranty of workmanlike performance.** New York implies a duty of workmanlike performance into residential construction contracts independent of express warranty language. Off-level cabinets, a cracked seam, loose tile, a vent into a cabinet, and a non-code outlet are textbook breaches. Redundant theory in case the court reads the express contract narrowly.

**Theory 6 — NYC Mechanical Code §504 venting.** Domestic kitchen exhaust ducts must terminate outside the building. Karras's hood vents into the upper cabinet — a clean §504 violation, independently actionable under Theories 1 and 5, and a discrete, photographable defect needing no expert to explain to Judge Vega.

## 4. Venue Strategy

Kings County Civil Court — Small Claims Part is the right forum. The cap is $10,000. Bremer's $14,200 estimate means recoverable cost-of-cure damages exceed the cap before we reach consequentials or §349. Claiming $7,500 is a deliberate election: at-or-near the cap (leaving headroom for whatever the judge might trim) and locking the case into small-claims rather than civil court. Four reasons in priority order:

1. **Speed.** Small-claims gets us a hearing ~six weeks from filing. Kings civil court is running 12+ months to first conference, more to trial. Wendell needs the kitchen functional before fall.
2. **Cost.** A flat $1,500 plus filing covers the small-claims path. Civil court would require an hourly arrangement the recoverable damages do not justify.
3. **Client preference.** Wendell explicitly asked for "the fastest path that gets me a check," subject to my ethical obligation to explain the waiver. He understood and initialed.
4. **Strategic denial of jury.** Karras would almost certainly demand a jury in civil court. Small-claims is bench, before a judge whose record we know.

**Election waiver risk.** Claiming $7,500 in small-claims waives recovery of the excess in this forum, and may collaterally estop us in any later forum on issues actually litigated. Wendell's informed consent is documented in the retainer, Article 4, with his initials. If Bremer's repairs come in over estimate, the delta is unrecoverable. This is the consumer's bargain for speed. (Damages math: **20_damages-calculation-research.md**.)

## 5. Damages Theory

Cost of cure $14,200 (Bremer, 2026-02-12), less unpaid balance $6,500 ($24,500 — $18,000 paid). Net direct damages $7,700. The $7,500 claim tracks cost-of-cure recovery just under the cap and anchors the case to a single document Aldous authenticates live in ~30 minutes. No need to prove consequentials (loss of use, takeout meals, spreadsheet rows 23–47) to reach $7,500 — clean to try. If Karras prevails on the $4,500 counterclaim (I do not expect this), net is $3,000 against $14,200 cure cost, still partly recoverable from the cap. Robust against the most likely adverse ruling.

## 6. Evidence Inventory

- **60 photos** from Wendell's phone, 2025-12-04 to 2026-01-22, time-stamped, before/during/after of each defect.
- **Contract** signed 2025-11-04, four pages.
- **Payment receipts**: deposit check 11-04, mid-project check 12-22, both cleared.
- **Bremer estimate** 2026-02-12, $14,200 on Bremer & Sons letterhead.
- **$4,500 change-order invoice** 2026-01-15.
- **Karras voicemail** of 2026-01-22 after the walk-off.
- **Karras–Wendell texts** across the project (Wendell will export the thread).
- **Margot Lévesque**, neighbor at 1610 Argyle Road, saw Karras's truck and overheard two arguments through the open kitchen window.
- **Wendell's spreadsheet**, "Kitchen Renovation 2025 - actual vs quoted," 47 rows.

**Photo curation.** Renee and I pick the top twelve for the exhibit binder, four per category (cabinets, quartz/tile, electrical/mechanical), prioritizing ones that show the defect plainly, include a tape measure or level for scale where applicable, and bear EXIF data we can authenticate. Tabs and a one-page index. The judge should see the case in five minutes.

**Witness plan.** Wendell testifies (clear, technical; the only risk is over-explanation — his civil-engineer training is a gift). Margot testifies live to duration and frequency of Karras's presence and the two overheard arguments including the 2026-01-22 walk-off. Aldous testifies as a fact witness on his estimate; deliberately *not* retained as expert because qualification adds nothing in small-claims, where Judge Vega routinely hears contractor estimates as fact testimony.

**Aldous credibility.** 30+ years in residential renovation; Bremer & Sons est. 1992; no prior relationship to Wendell (referred independently); shop at 4128 18th Avenue, Brooklyn. Will appear in work clothes — fine for this room.

## 7. Weaknesses

(a) **The oral $4,500 change order.** Karras claims Wendell verbally approved a change for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet." No smoking-gun text from Wendell saying "no." Disproving an oral approval is structurally hard absent a written record. Mitigated by GBL §771 below.

(b) **"Trade tolerance."** Karras will argue the 1/2-inch out-of-level on the south run is "within trade tolerance (1/4–1/2 inch)." Some industry sources do reference quarter- to half-inch tolerances; we need to be precise about the standard.

(c) **"Settling building."** The brownstone is 1920s. Karras will argue the loose tile and grout cracking is settlement, "normal in old buildings." Surface plausibility for an older building.

(d) **Range hood verbal discussion.** Karras claims exterior venting was "to be discussed with electrician but never confirmed by Wendell." No email confirming hood scope, only the contract's general line.

## 8. Counter-Strategy

**Against the oral change order: GBL §771.** NY GBL §771 requires home-improvement contracts and any changes to be in writing for HIC contractors. An oral change order on a residential job is unenforceable against the consumer. Karras's $4,500 counterclaim is therefore vulnerable on pure statutory law before we reach the factual question of whether Wendell authorized anything. The single strongest counter-argument in the case.

**Against trade tolerance.** NAHB Residential Construction Performance Guidelines — routinely cited by industry tribunals — set a maximum of 1/4 inch over 32 inches for cabinet level. A half-inch deviation on a continuous run exceeds the NAHB standard outright. Photo with a four-foot level makes it concrete; even without the published standard, a half-inch tilt in a finished kitchen is not "trade tolerance" by any consumer-facing measure.

**Against the settling-building defense.** Wendell's photo timestamps show grout cracking and tile movement within thirty days of installation. Settlement of a 1920s brownstone occurs over years; a thirty-day window does not fit the defense's own theory of slow movement. We pre-empt with EXIF data and the spreadsheet rows showing the date he first noticed each defect.

**Against the range hood.** NYC Mechanical Code §504 runs to the contractor regardless of conversation. Even if Wendell verbally said "skip the venting" (no evidence he did), the instruction would not relieve Karras of code compliance. One of the cleanest defects in the case.

## 9. Settlement Posture

Floor **$5,000** (per retainer, Article 6 — initialed). Aspirational **$7,500** (full claim). Either way settlement is conditioned on full mutual release and clean walkaway — no counterclaim survival, no warranty work resumption, no future contact. Wendell does not want Karras back in the house under any circumstances.

I anticipate counsel will open with $3,000–$3,500 around the discovery exchange. The Forest Hills construction-defense bar tends to test the floor before discovery responses are due. Reject anything below $5,000 absent a meaningful concession on costs (Aldous's appearance fee, filing). Accept $5,000–$6,000 only with full release. Above $6,000 is a clear settle. Hearing-week numbers shift upward as Karras's live-witness costs become real; that's the leverage point I press on or about 2026-03-17.

## 10. Predictive — Opposing Counsel

Karras retains within ~two weeks of complaint service. The Forest Hills construction-defense bar is small. Based on prior patterns from that part — including two 2024 matters — **Felipe Ortega** of Ortega Law Office (71-15 Austin St, Forest Hills) is plausible counsel. Ortega is generally cooperative, civil practice, construction-defense focus; standard pre-hearing posture is a single low offer and an answer with general denial plus a kitchen-sink counterclaim. Not locked; we assume whoever appears moves similarly.

## 11. Counterclaim Risk

Expect a $4,500 counterclaim. On the merits, GBL §771 renders an oral home-improvement change unenforceable against a consumer. There is no writing. Karras's only path is to reframe the work as outside-scope unjust enrichment, which fails because (i) the work was not actually completed (hardware and outlet are entangled with the disputed scope), and (ii) the consumer-protection regime does not permit unjust-enrichment end-runs around §771. Unlikely to prevail.

## 12. Action Plan with Dates

- **2026-02-16 (Mon).** Draft demand letter; outline exists.
- **2026-02-19 (Thu).** Mail demand letter certified to Karras; email courtesy copy. Five business days for substantive response.
- **2026-02-24 (Tue).** Response window expires.
- **2026-02-26 (Thu).** File complaint at Kings County Civil Court Small Claims Part if no substantive response. $20 filing fee (money order).
- **2026-03-05 (Thu).** Serve discovery — document requests plus five interrogatories.
- **2026-03-09 (Mon).** Witness interview with Margot Lévesque at 1610 Argyle Road.
- **2026-03-10 (Tue).** Witness interview with Aldous Bremer at 4128 18th Avenue.
- **2026-03-15 (Sun).** Hearing-prep outline drafted. *NB — Sunday 03-15 conflicts w/ Prospect Park soccer; will draft Sat night.*
- **2026-03-17 (Tue).** Pre-hearing prep meeting with Wendell, 90 minutes.
- **2026-03-19 (Thu).** Final document organization; exhibit binder finalized.
- **2026-03-20 (Fri).** First hearing, Part 5, 9:30 AM, before Hon. Marisol Vega.

## 13. Judge — Hon. Marisol Vega

Per three prior appearances in Part 5: no-nonsense, evidence-driven, runs the calendar tight, dislikes hearsay objections in small-claims (relaxed rules; she moves past them quickly). Likes parties arriving with a tabbed exhibit binder, a one-page chronology, and a damages number that ties to a document in the binder. Disfavors prolonged direct on background; rewards witnesses who answer the question asked. Prep Wendell accordingly.

## 14. Pre-Hearing Motion Analysis

Small-claims does not permit summary judgment; dispositive motion practice is functionally unavailable. The case is decided at the 03-20 hearing on testimony and the exhibit binder. Discovery disputes raised orally at the start of the hearing if meet-and-confer fails.

## 15. Insurance Recovery Alternative

Declined. Wendell is insured through Allstate; deductible exceeds the claim and coverage does not contemplate construction-defect first-party recovery. Burns time without proportionate return.

## 16. BBB and Background

Karras's BBB record: two prior complaints, both resolved. I have flagged pulling underlying records for possible impeachment if Karras testifies inconsistently, but will not introduce them as exhibits unless clearly probative. No need to dirty the record with collateral matter when the merits are clean.

## 17. Demand Letter Timing

Mailing 2026-02-19 gives Karras five business days (a standard pre-suit window I observe even where statute does not require it). The window expires 2026-02-24, allowing complaint filing on 2026-02-26 with a clean record of pre-suit notice. Certified-mail receipt and any returned green card go into the file.

## 18. Discovery Strategy

Small-claims is informal; no Article 31 machinery. I serve my own document requests (contract, change-order invoice, all texts and emails between Karras and Wendell 2025-11-04 through 2026-01-22, license records, sub-vendor invoices including Crystallo Surfaces batch QS-2025-1182) and five interrogatories targeting (i) the alleged oral approval, (ii) any writing of the change order, (iii) basis for "trade tolerance," (iv) basis for blaming the quartz manufacturer, and (v) Karras's account of the walk-off. Expect resistance on text messages — the most damaging category for Karras — and flag meet-and-confer immediately if production is incomplete.

## 19. Settlement Triggers

Anticipate $3,000–$3,500 from opposing side around week-5 discovery exchange. Reject below $5,000 absent cost concessions tied to live-witness expenses Karras would otherwise incur. Above $6,000 with full release is a clear yes.

## 20. Ethical Note

Per NY Rule 4.2, once Karras retains counsel all communication routes through counsel. No direct contact with Karras. Renee has been instructed; policy is in the matter folder.

## 21. Communication Plan

Weekly status update to Wendell on Thursdays, phone or short email per his preference. Same-day response on hearing-week issues; anything received Thursday 03-19 or Friday 03-20 morning gets handled before the 9:30 call. Yuki is not a party and will not be copied on confidential communications absent Wendell's explicit written request.

## 22. Open Questions

### Procedural Reminders — Small Claims Part

1. **Informal forum.** The Small Claims Part is an informal forum. The strict rules of evidence (CPLR Article 45) are relaxed; the Court will receive any evidence that, in its judgment, is material and competent. Hearsay objections are noted but rarely sustained where the proffered statement bears reasonable indicia of reliability.

2. **Witnesses.** Each party may present witnesses. Witnesses must testify under oath. Subpoenas, if needed, must be issued and served not less than two (2) days before the hearing per NYCCCA § 1812. Friendly witnesses appearing voluntarily need not be subpoenaed.

3. **Documentary evidence — three sets.** All documentary exhibits should be presented in **three (3) sets**: one for the Court, one for the opposing side, and one for the offering party's own use during examination. Pre-marking exhibits (Plaintiff's Exhibit 1, 2, 3 …; Defendant's Exhibit A, B, C …) is strongly preferred and will expedite the call.

4. **No recording — phones off.** Recording of any kind in the courtroom is **prohibited**. All cellular telephones, smart watches, tablets, and personal electronic devices must be silenced or turned off. Hon. Vega further requires **airplane mode** be engaged for any device that remains on a counsel-table or in a juror-box seat. Violations may result in confiscation by the court officer and contempt proceedings.

5. **Arrival and screening.** Parties and counsel should arrive by **9:00 AM** to clear security screening at 141 Livingston Street. The screening line at peak hours can take 20–25 minutes; allowance should be made. Sharp objects, large bags, food, and beverages other than sealed water are subject to inspection or refusal.

6. **Interpreter services.** Limited Court-provided interpreter services are available. A request must be submitted to the Clerk's Office not less than **five (5) business days** before the hearing. **No interpreter has been requested in this matter.** Should a need arise, parties must promptly notify the Clerk's Office at (347) 404-9123.

7. **Settlement discussions.** Counsel and pro se parties are encouraged to confer in the hallway outside Room 502 prior to calendar call. If a settlement is reached, **report it to the court officer at calendar call** so the matter may be marked accordingly. The Court welcomes stipulations of settlement on the record.

8. **No jury.** **Jury demand is not available** in the Small Claims Part. All matters are tried as bench trials before the assigned judge.

9. **Right of appeal.** A judgment of the Small Claims Part may be appealed to the Appellate Term of the Supreme Court, Second Department, **within thirty (30) days** of entry of judgment. The standard of review is whether substantial justice has been done between the parties according to the rules and principles of substantive law (NYCCCA § 1807).

10. **Decorum.** Business or business-casual attire is expected. Hats are removed in the courtroom (religious head coverings excepted). Eating, gum, and audible side conversations are not permitted.

## 4. Interrogatory Answers

### Interrogatory 1 — Identify all individuals who performed work on the Project, with role and contact.

**Answer.** The following individuals performed work on the Park kitchen renovation project at 1612 Argyle Road:

1. **Stefan Karras** — Owner / lead carpenter, Karras Custom Builders LLC. Present 24 of the working days (see Interrogatory 5).
2. **Yannis Pappas** — Laborer, employee of Karras Custom Builders LLC. Demolition, hauling, basic prep. Present approximately 9 working days.
3. **Andreas Vasilakos** — Finish carpenter, employee of Karras Custom Builders LLC. Cabinet hang, trim, scribing. Present approximately 11 working days.
4. **Pavlos Stamatopoulos** — Master electrician, NY license **#EL-449821**, subcontractor. Performed all electrical work, including the GFCI / non-GFCI outlet near the sink. Present 2 days (rough, 2025-12-15; final, 2026-01-09).

No other employees, day-laborers, or subs performed work on this project. No individuals from Brooklyn Cabinetry Co., Crystallo Surfaces, Tile World, or Bay Ridge Appliance Outlet performed installation work; their roles were strictly supply.

### Interrogatory 2 — State all facts supporting the alleged $4,500 change order.

**Answer.** On or about **December 18, 2025**, between approximately **11:00 AM and 12:00 PM**, in the kitchen at **1612 Argyle Road**, Stefan Karras and Wendell Park had a conversation regarding two upgrades:

(a) substituting the standard cabinet hardware with an upgraded soft-close, brushed-nickel hardware set across all 22 cabinet doors and drawer fronts; and

(b) adding **one (1) additional duplex outlet** at the kitchen island, which was not on the contract drawings.

Mr. Karras represents that he priced the combined upgrades verbally at approximately **$4,500**, that Mr. Park said words to the effect of **"go ahead"** or **"yes, do it,"** and that Mr. Karras then proceeded to order the upgraded hardware and to schedule the additional electrical work. **No witnesses other than Stefan Karras and Wendell Park were present.** The only contemporaneous documentary trace is the handwritten note produced as **KCB-000013**, plus the invoice transmitted on 2026-01-15 (KCB-000016). Mr. Karras concedes that the matter ultimately rests on **"Wendell's word"** as against Mr. Karras's word.

### Interrogatory 3 — Identify the quartz countertop manufacturer, batch, warranty, and any communications regarding the seam crack.

**Answer.** Manufacturer: **Crystallo Surfaces**. Batch: **QS-2025-1182**. Warranty terms: 1-year manufacturer's limited warranty, excluding "stress fractures attributable to substrate movement, improper installation by third party, or post-install impact damage." Warranty document is attached to the produced invoice (**KCB-000018**).

Communications with Crystallo regarding the seam crack: Mr. Karras represents that **two emails** were exchanged with Crystallo's customer-service line after the seam crack was reported, and that he forwarded both onward to Wendell Park. The exact dates are not currently located in his archive; he believes both occurred between **2026-01-08** and **2026-01-20**. Defendant will supplement if and when the emails are recovered.

### Interrogatory 4 — GFCI installation near the kitchen sink; any deviations from NYC electrical code.

**Answer.** The contract scope included **one (1) GFCI outlet** within the code-required reach of the kitchen sink, to be installed by **Pavlos Stamatopoulos** (NY license **#EL-449821**). Mr. Karras represents that, during a kitchen walk-through with Mr. Park (date not precisely recalled, in the approximate window of the 2025-12-18 conversation referenced in Interrogatory 2), Mr. Park asked him to **substitute a standard duplex outlet** for the GFCI **"for aesthetic reasons,"** as Mr. Park disliked the visible test/reset buttons on the splashback. Mr. Karras relayed this to Mr. Stamatopoulos, who installed a standard duplex.

**This characterization is disputed by plaintiff.** Defendant produces no documentation — written request, email, text, signed waiver, or contemporaneous note — supporting the substitution. Mr. Stamatopoulos's invoice annotation ("1 GFCI omitted per HO request — see attached note") refers to a note that is not produced.

### Interrogatory 5 — Days Stefan Karras was personally present on site; communications regarding range-hood venting.

**Answer.** Mr. Karras was personally present on **24 of the working days** between 2025-12-01 and 2026-01-22, as reflected in the produced daily logs (KCB-000025 to KCB-000040). On the remaining days, Mr. Pappas and/or Mr. Vasilakos were on site without him.

Regarding range-hood venting: Mr. Karras represents that proper exterior venting "was discussed but not finalized" with Mr. Park. He represents that he raised, on at least one occasion, that exterior venting through the brick rear wall would require a separate mechanical permit and a visible duct run, and that an interior recirculating arrangement was an alternative; he represents that **Mr. Park did not confirm a path forward** and the range hood was installed without an exterior duct connection in the absence of further direction. Mr. Karras defers to Mr. Park's testimony as to when this conversation occurred.

## A. CASE THEME (memorize — open and close on this)

> Wendell Park hired a licensed contractor to do a competent kitchen renovation. He paid $18,000. He got a half-finished, code-violating result. He's owed $7,500 — a fraction of his actual repair cost — to make him whole.

Subordinate themes (use only if Vega asks a follow-up):
- This is a workmanship case, not a taste case. Defects are measurable.
- The change-order claim is the defense's whole pillar; it has no writing behind it. GBL §771 does the rest.
- We are deliberately under-claiming. The independent estimate is $14,200; we ask $7,500. That is itself a credibility move.

Tone: calm, factual, slightly understated. Vega reportedly dislikes oratory; she wants chronology and numbers. Direct concise. Cross short. No theatrics.

## B. OPENING STATEMENT OUTLINE (3 minutes max — strictly)

Purpose: orient Vega, plant the four landmarks, and sit down.

1. **Contract.** Signed 2025-11-04 between Wendell Park and Karras Custom Builders LLC. Total contract price $24,500. Scope: cabinet replacement (custom shaker maple), quartz countertops, porcelain floor tile, electrical updates including code-mandated GFCI outlets near the sink. Start 2025-12-01. Promised completion 2026-01-15. (Tab 1.)

2. **Defects discovered in January 2026.** First defect — countertop crack along the seam — visible 2026-01-08. Cabinets off-level by 1/2 inch on the south wall run. Roughly six floor tiles loose; grout cracked in two areas. Outlet next to the sink not GFCI — NYC code violation. Range hood vents into the cabinet above, not the exterior. Karras walked off the job 2026-01-22 after argument over a $4,500 change-order invoice Wendell never agreed to in writing.

3. **The independent number.** Aldous Bremer of Bremer & Sons, on letterhead, walked the kitchen and put repair cost in writing on 2026-02-12 at **$14,200**. (Tab 4.) Wendell claims **$7,500** — to keep the matter in the small-claims part rather than civil court, and because he simply wants the kitchen made right.

4. **Change-order claim.** Defense will say Wendell verbally approved $4,500 mid-project for "upgraded cabinet hardware and an additional outlet." There is no writing. There is no signed change order, no email, no text. New York General Business Law §771 requires home-improvement change orders in writing. The claim is unenforceable on its face.

Close opening with: "We will show you the contract, the photos, the estimate, and the absence of any writing. Then we'll ask you to make Wendell Park whole."

## Defect-by-Defect Q&A

### Q4 — Cabinets off-level

**CO:** Defect one — cabinets off-level. What did you find?
**AB:** I measured a half-inch rise across an 84-inch run on the south wall. Used the Bosch on a tripod, shot the line, measured down to the cabinet edge at eight points along the run. The high point was at the east end, near the range. Half-inch over 84 inches. Industry tolerance — and I'll give you a written cite if you want — is a quarter-inch maximum across 32 inches for upper cabinets, and roughly equivalent for base. Karras's run is twice the tolerance. You can see it without a level if you look at the reveal between the cabinet bottom and the countertop; it grows from a hair on one end to almost a quarter inch on the other.

**CO:** Cost to correct?
**AB:** Three thousand two hundred dollars, $3,200. That's pulling face frames, re-shimming the carcasses, re-mounting through the back rail, and re-aligning the doors. Doors I can re-hang with the existing hinges if they're cup-style adjustable; if not, new hinges add maybe forty dollars in parts. Labor's the bulk of it — call it twenty-eight crew-hours.

**CO:** Karras claims this is "within trade tolerance, one-quarter to one-half inch."
**AB:** That's not a tolerance any trade group I know publishes. NKBA, AWI, KCMA — none of them give half-inch as acceptable for an 84-inch run. He's quoting himself.

### Q5 — Countertop crack

**CO:** Defect two — quartz countertop crack.
**AB:** Crystallo brand, 3-centimeter slab, eased edge. Crack runs along the seam between the two slabs that meet just to the left of the sink cutout. About fourteen inches long. I looked at it under a flashlight and a 10x loupe. It is not a manufacturer defect. The pattern of the crack tracks the seam line, and the failure starts right where the seam meets the sink-cutout corner — that corner should have a pin or a rod carrying the load across the seam. Karras epoxied the seam without proper rod or pin support. The corner is the highest-stress point in any countertop install, and it's the first place a bad seam fails.

**CO:** Cost to correct?
**AB:** Replace the cracked half plus a new seam. Four thousand eight hundred dollars, $4,800. That includes the slab, the template, the cut, the install, the seam materials, and demo and disposal of the cracked piece. I assume the surviving half is in good shape; if not, the number goes up.

### Q6 — Manufacturer warranty

**CO:** Karras blames the supplier — Crystallo Surfaces, batch QS-2025-1182. Manufacturer warranty?
**AB:** Manufacturer warranty covers material defect — voids in the slab, color irregularities, structural failure that originates in the material itself. It does not cover installation. This crack is at the seam, which by definition is something the installer creates on site. Karras can't pin this on Crystallo. I'd expect Crystallo to take one look and decline. If you want, I can give you the name of the rep at Crystallo's Long Island City fabrication partner; he's straight-up and he'll say the same thing on a call.

### Q7 — Floor tile

**CO:** Defect three — floor tile.
**AB:** Six tiles I could lift by hand. Not pry, lift — they came up with finger pressure. Grout cracking in two zones, one along the run between the island and the range, the other under the sink. That is not settling. Settling takes years to manifest in a brownstone of that age, and when it does it cracks along stress lines that radiate from a load-bearing wall, not in the patterns I saw. What I saw is bad mortar coverage — the installer back-buttered some tiles and not others, or skipped notching with the trowel in a hurry. Re-set: $1,650. That includes pulling the loose tiles and the four around them, scraping mortar, re-setting with proper coverage, regrout the affected zones.

**CO:** Karras says it's settling, normal in old buildings.
**AB:** Building's a hundred-and-some years old. If it had moved enough in the last sixty days to crack new tile, you'd have plaster cracks on the second floor. There aren't any.

### Q8 — GFCI

**CO:** Defect four — GFCI outlet.
**AB:** I measured. The outlet next to the sink is within thirty inches of the sink edge. Code requires GFCI for any receptacle within six feet of the sink edge, kitchen, full stop. NEC 210.8(A)(7) and the City's amendments. This one is a standard duplex, not GFCI. I confirmed it isn't on a GFCI breaker upstream by checking the panel — Karras pulled the electrical permit so the panel directory is partly labeled. **CO:** Karras says he installed an "additional outlet" as part of the change order.

**CO:** Defect five — range hood.
**AB:** This one is the worst. The vent terminates inside the upper cabinet directly above the range. There is no exterior duct. It's a fire and grease hazard — you accumulate grease in the cabinet, you ignite a stovetop fire, you have a chase straight up into wood. It also defeats the purpose of the hood. To fix: cut the exterior wall, run rigid metal duct to a wall cap, seal, and re-trim. Two thousand nine hundred fifty dollars, $2,950. You need a mechanical permit. I priced the permit and inspection inside that number.

**CO:** Karras says the range-hood vent termination was "an item to be discussed with electrician but never confirmed by Wendell."

I spent the last four minutes coaching Aldous on cross-examination posture, in the event Ortega forces him over.

## Substantive Q&A

**Q1 (Carmen):** How often did you observe Mr. Karras's truck on your block during the renovation period?
**A:** Most weekdays, December through mid-January. White Ford F-250 — full-size pickup — with the Karras Custom Builders logo on the door, the one with the hammer-and-house silhouette. He parked usually in the no-parking-Tuesday-Thursday spot directly across from 1612, but he moved it on cleaning days. I noticed because that spot is contested; the woman at 1615 has fought with people over it for years. Karras, to his credit, was respectful of the alternate-side schedule.

**Q1a:** Did you ever see the truck on weekends?
**A:** Once, a Saturday, I think the second weekend of December. Not regularly, though. Weekdays were the pattern.

**Q2:** Did you observe any work activity through their kitchen window?
**A:** Through their kitchen window — sometimes, yes. Not constantly; I wasn't watching, I was living my life. But I saw cabinets going in around mid-December — there were a couple of days where I could see two men hoisting the upper cabinets, holding them in place while a third one drilled. Then the countertop installation around Christmas week — I remember because I was making a tourtière and I looked up and saw them sliding a big slab in. Two pieces, I think. They had suction-cup handles on it.

**Q2a:** Did the work appear, to your lay observation, to be done with care or in a rush?
**A:** I'm not a contractor. But the cabinet day looked methodical. The countertop day — they were laughing a lot, which I don't know how to interpret. Could be camaraderie, could be sloppy. I genuinely don't know.

**Q3:** Did you ever speak directly with Mr. Karras?
**A:** Once, briefly, in early December. I was bringing in groceries from the curb — a paper bag was splitting — and he was carrying tile boxes from the truck. He nodded. I said, "Looks like a big job." He said, "They always are." That was it. Polite. Not warm.

**Q4:** Did you observe any arguments between Mr. Park and Mr. Karras?
**A:** Yes — two times I remember clearly.

**Q4a — First argument, Margot's account:**
*"Around mid-January, maybe the 15th or 16th. Their kitchen window was open — Wendell had it open for ventilation; that range hood wasn't doing much, I now realize, knowing what I know now. Voices raised. Wendell was saying 'this isn't what we agreed' and a man's voice — Karras — said something like 'you're nickel-and-diming me.' That phrase stuck with me because it's old-fashioned. The argument lasted maybe five minutes. I remember it because Lucy" — she gestured at the smaller cat — "got under the couch, which she does when there's tension. Wendell's voice has never been raised in seven years that I've heard. So when it was, it registered."*

**Q4a-i:** Are you confident on the date?
**A:** Reasonably confident on mid-January. I'd want to look at my journal to pin it.

**Q4b — Second argument, Margot's account:**
*"Walk-off day, I think — January 22. Same scenario, kitchen window cracked open even though it was cold. Wendell was angry about an invoice — he used the word 'invoice' specifically, more than once. Karras said 'forget it, I'm done.' Then a truck door slammed — the F-250 has a heavy door, a particular sound — and he drove off. I made a note in my journal that night because I'd never seen Wendell stand on his stoop afterwards looking like that. He just stood there in the cold without a coat, I think for ten minutes."*

**Q5:** Do you keep a journal?
**A:** Yes, daily. Five-line journal — I started during the pandemic. It's a habit now. Just a few sentences a night before bed. I have entries for both days.

**Q6:** Would you consent to providing your journal entries from those two dates?
**A:** Yes, the relevant lines only — I'd rather not produce the whole thing. There's personal material in there. But the lines for those two days, absolutely, you can have those.

7. **¶ 7 (cabinet defect).** **DENIED.** Defendants affirmatively allege that the cabinet level is within trade tolerance and not a defect (see Affirmative Defense 2).
8. **¶ 8 (countertop crack).** **DENIED** as to Defendants' responsibility. Defendants affirmatively allege that the crack is a manufacturer defect arising from the supplier's batch (see Affirmative Defense 3).
9. **¶ 9 (floor tile).** **DENIED.** Defendants affirmatively allege the loose tiles and grout cracking are attributable to settling normal in older buildings (see Affirmative Defense 4).
10. **¶ 10 (GFCI outlet).** Defendants **DENY** that any installed outlet adjacent to the sink violates NYC Electrical Code; to the extent any outlet was installed without GFCI protection, it is denied that such installation was within the agreed-upon scope as performed and completed by Defendants prior to the alleged 2026-01-22 termination.
11. **¶ 11 (range hood).** **DENIED.** Defendants affirmatively allege the venting solution was an open item to be discussed with the electrician and never confirmed by Plaintiff (see Affirmative Defense 5).
12. **¶ 12 (change order).** **DENIED** as to the allegation that the $4,500 change order was "oral-only" without authority; **DENIED** that Plaintiff did not approve it. Defendants affirmatively allege Plaintiff verbally approved the change order on 2025-12-18 (see Affirmative Defense 1 and Counterclaim).
13. **¶ 13 (walk-off).** **DENIED** as characterized; Defendants admit work ceased on the project after 2026-01-22 but **DENY** that this constituted a "walk-off" in any actionable sense, and affirmatively allege that Plaintiff's refusal to remit the agreed change-order amount constituted a material breach by Plaintiff that excused further performance.
14. **¶ 14 (damages — $7,500).** **DENIED.** Defendants deny any liability to Plaintiff in any amount and specifically deny the propriety of the Bremer & Sons repair estimate as a measure of damages under New York law.

## II. Affirmative Defenses

Defendants assert the following affirmative defenses, each of which is hereby pleaded and reserved:

**FIRST AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Approved Change Order.**
On or about **2025-12-18**, during a mid-project site visit at 1612 Argyle Road, Plaintiff Wendell Park orally approved a change order in the amount of **$4,500** for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet." Defendants reasonably relied upon Plaintiff's approval, ordered and supplied the upgraded Italian-made cabinet hardware (pulls and hinges) and installed one (1) additional 20-amp outlet near the pantry in accordance with that approval. Plaintiff is bound by his approval and is liable for the agreed change-order amount.

**SECOND AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Trade Tolerance.**
The cabinet level along the south-wall run is within industry trade tolerance of one-quarter inch to one-half inch (1/4"–1/2") per NAHB Residential Construction Performance Guidelines. Such variation is *not a defect* and is consistent with customary practice in pre-war Brooklyn brownstones with non-plumb structural conditions, including 1612 Argyle Road, a 1920s-era structure.

**THIRD AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Manufacturer Warranty / Third-Party Defect.**
The crack alleged in the quartz countertop is, on information and belief, a manufacturer defect. The countertop slab originated from supplier **Crystallo Surfaces** under batch number **QS-2025-1182**. A manufacturer warranty is available to Plaintiff and was tendered to him by Defendants, who offered to coordinate the warranty claim. Plaintiff declined to pursue the warranty. Liability for the crack, if any, lies with Crystallo Surfaces, not with Defendants.

**FOURTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Building Settlement.**
Plaintiff's residence at 1612 Argyle Road is a 1920s brownstone subject to ordinary settling and seasonal substrate movement. The loose floor tiles and grout cracking complained of are attributable to such settling, not to any deficiency in Defendants' workmanship. Defendants are not insurers against settlement of pre-existing structures.

**FIFTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Open Scope Item (Range Hood).**
The exterior venting of the range hood was, at all relevant times, an open scope item to be coordinated with the electrician retained for the project. Plaintiff was advised of this open status but never confirmed a scope or routing for the exterior vent. Defendants cannot be held liable for failure to perform work that was never confirmed within scope.

**SIXTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Failure to Mitigate.**
Plaintiff failed to mitigate any alleged damages by refusing Defendants' good-faith offer to complete a punch-list resolution upon payment of the agreed $4,500 change order. Plaintiff's refusal to permit Defendants to cure forecloses recovery for items that could have been remedied at original contract cost.

**SEVENTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Plaintiff's Prior Material Breach.**
Plaintiff's claim is barred, in whole or in part, by his own prior material breach of the contract, namely his refusal to remit the $4,500 due under the approved change order. A party in material breach may not recover for a counter-party's subsequent non-performance excused by that breach.

**EIGHTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Notice and Limitations.**
Plaintiff's claim is barred, in whole or in part, by his failure to comply with notice and cure provisions reflected at clause 14 of the parties' contract dated 2025-11-04, and by applicable contractual and statutory limitations on timing and form of notice.

**NINTH AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE — Claim-Splitting.**
Plaintiff has elected to file in the Small Claims Part with a stated demand of **$7,500**, at or near the statutory cap. To the extent Plaintiff alleges damages exceeding that amount (the Bremer & Sons estimate references $14,200), Defendants plead defensively that Plaintiff has waived recovery above the cap, and any subsequent action seeking the difference would be barred by claim-splitting. Nothing in this defense is an admission of liability.

## III. Counterclaim

1. The parties entered into a written contract dated 2025-11-04 for kitchen renovation services at 1612 Argyle Road, Brooklyn NY 11218.
2. On or about **2025-12-18**, during a mid-project site visit at 1612 Argyle Road, Plaintiff and Stefan Karras discussed an upgrade to the cabinet hardware and the addition of one (1) outlet near the pantry.

STATEMENT OF CLAIM

1. JURISDICTION AND VENUE. This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to Article 18 of the New York City Civil Court Act (NYCCCA §§ 1801–1814), governing the Small Claims Part. The amount in controversy, $7,500.00, does not exceed the $10,000.00 jurisdictional limit of the Small Claims Part. Venue is properly laid in Kings County because Defendants maintain their principal place of business in Kings County, the contract at issue was substantially performed in Kings County, and Plaintiff resides in Kings County at 1612 Argyle Road, Brooklyn, NY 11226 (Ditmas Park).

2. THE PARTIES. Plaintiff Wendell Park is a natural person residing at 1612 Argyle Road, Brooklyn, New York 11226, and the sole record owner of that property since 2017. Defendant Karras Custom Builders LLC is a New York limited liability company organized in 2019 and registered with the New York Department of State, with its principal place of business at 8412 4th Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11209. Defendant Stefan Karras, age 53, resides in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, and is the sole member and managing officer of Karras Custom Builders LLC. At all relevant times, Defendant Karras held New York City Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) License No. 1374829, issued by the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

3. THE CONTRACT. On November 4, 2025, Plaintiff and Defendant Stefan Karras (on behalf of Karras Custom Builders LLC) executed a written home-improvement contract for a complete kitchen renovation of the subject premises (the "Contract"), at a total price of Twenty-Four Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($24,500.00). The agreed scope included: (a) demolition and removal of existing cabinetry, countertops, flooring, and selected fixtures; (b) custom shaker-style maple cabinetry; (c) quartz countertops sourced from Crystallo Surfaces; (d) porcelain floor tile and grout with associated underlayment; (e) electrical updates including a code-mandated GFCI-protected receptacle adjacent to the kitchen sink per the NYC Electrical Code; and (f) reconnection and exterior venting of the existing range hood. A true and correct copy of the Contract is on file as Exhibit A and referenced herein but not annexed inline.

4. PAYMENTS MADE. The Contract established a three-installment payment schedule: (i) an Eight Thousand Dollar ($8,000.00) deposit due at signing; (ii) Eight Thousand Dollars ($8,000.00) due at the mid-project milestone; and (iii) Eight Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($8,500.00) due upon substantial completion. Plaintiff paid (i) on November 4, 2025 (deposit, by personal check), and (ii) on December 22, 2025 (mid-project, by personal check), for a total of Eighteen Thousand Dollars ($18,000.00) actually paid to Defendants. Plaintiff has not paid the third installment of $8,500.00, that installment having never become due because Defendants did not substantially or even minimally complete the work in conformity with the Contract.

5. PROMISED COMPLETION AND ABANDONMENT. The Contract specified a project start date of December 1, 2025 and a promised completion date of January 15, 2026. As of January 15, 2026, the work was not complete and contained the material defects described below. On January 22, 2026, following an in-person dispute concerning a purported $4,500.00 add-on invoice (described in Paragraph 6), Defendant Stefan Karras walked off the job site, removed his tools and materials from the premises, and ceased all further performance under the Contract. Defendants have not returned to the property and have not offered to cure any of the defects.

6. THE DISPUTED ALLEGED CHANGE ORDER. On or about January 15, 2026, Defendant Karras tendered an invoice to Plaintiff for an additional $4,500.00, claiming this amount was owed for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet" pursuant to an alleged oral change order to which Plaintiff had purportedly agreed. Plaintiff disputes that any such oral agreement was reached and disputes that the invoiced items were ever delivered or installed in upgraded form. Any oral modification of a residential home-improvement contract is unenforceable for failure to comply with New York General Business Law § 771, which requires home-improvement contracts and any amendments thereto to be in writing and signed by both parties. Plaintiff therefore refused to pay the $4,500.00 invoice and continues to refuse.

7. DEFECT NO. 1 — CABINETS OFF-LEVEL. The custom maple shaker cabinets installed by Defendants on the south wall run of the kitchen are out of level by approximately one-half inch (1/2") across the full run, as measured by Plaintiff with a four-foot construction level on multiple occasions and as confirmed by the inspection of Aldous Bremer (Bremer & Sons) on February 12, 2026. The deviation is plainly visible to the naked eye, causes upper-cabinet doors to swing closed under gravity, and creates a visible reveal at the countertop interface. Defendant Karras has asserted that this deviation falls "within trade tolerance (1/4"–1/2")"; that assertion is rejected, both because the deviation is at the outer edge of the range Defendant himself cites and because it produces a non-functional installation.

8. DEFECT NO. 2 — QUARTZ COUNTERTOP CRACK. The quartz countertop installed by Defendants developed a visible crack along the seam joining the two principal slabs, which crack was first observed and photographed by Plaintiff on January 8, 2026, within three weeks of installation. The countertop was supplied by Crystallo Surfaces, batch number QS-2025-1182. Defendant Karras has asserted that the crack is the responsibility of the manufacturer under warranty; Plaintiff has investigated this defense and learned that Crystallo Surfaces' written warranty expressly excludes cracking caused by improper seam preparation, inadequate substrate support, or installer error, all of which are at issue here. Plaintiff therefore alleges the crack is the result of Defendants' defective workmanship at the seam and not of any latent defect in the quartz material itself.

9. DEFECT NO. 3 — LOOSE FLOOR TILES AND CRACKING GROUT. Approximately six (6) of the porcelain floor tiles installed by Defendants are loose and rock under foot pressure, indicating either failure of the tile mortar bond or inadequate substrate preparation. In addition, the grout between tiles is cracked in two distinct areas, one near the refrigerator pad and one in the entryway between the kitchen and dining room. Defendant Karras has asserted that these conditions constitute "settling, normal in old buildings"; Plaintiff rejects that explanation, both because the building's structure has been stable throughout Plaintiff's nine years of ownership and because the defects appeared within weeks of installation, not over a period consistent with structural settlement.

10. DEFECT NO. 4 — NON-GFCI OUTLET (CODE VIOLATION). Defendants installed a standard, non-GFCI electrical receptacle adjacent to the kitchen sink, in direct violation of the New York City Electrical Code, which requires GFCI (ground-fault circuit-interrupter) protection for all receptacles serving countertop surfaces in dwelling unit kitchens and within six feet of any sink. The Contract expressly included "code-mandated GFCI outlets near sink" within its scope. Defendants both failed to perform this work as contracted and created a code-noncompliant condition presenting a documented risk of electrical shock in a wet area.

11. DEFECT NO. 5 — RANGE HOOD NOT VENTED TO EXTERIOR. The kitchen range hood reinstalled by Defendants is not connected to any exterior ductwork; instead, the hood discharges directly into the closed cabinet space immediately above it. This installation method violates the New York City Mechanical Code § 504, which requires that domestic kitchen exhaust be discharged directly to the outdoors through a duct of approved material with a backdraft damper. Defendant Karras has asserted that exterior venting was "an item to be discussed with the electrician but never confirmed by Wendell"; this assertion is contradicted by the express written scope of the Contract, which lists "reconnect and vent range hood to exterior" as an included item. The current installation creates a fire and indoor-air-quality hazard.

12. PRE-SUIT DEMAND. By certified letter and email dated February 19, 2026, undersigned counsel served on Defendants a written demand setting forth the foregoing defects, the calculation of damages, and a five-business-day window for substantive response. The certified letter was signed for by Defendant Stefan Karras on February 23, 2026, per the USPS return receipt (green card). The window expired on February 24, 2026, with no substantive response from either Defendant.

13. INDEPENDENT REPAIR ESTIMATE. On February 12, 2026, Aldous Bremer of Bremer & Sons (4128 18th Avenue, Brooklyn, NY) inspected the subject kitchen and provided Plaintiff with a written, line-itemized repair estimate, on Bremer & Sons letterhead, in the total amount of Fourteen Thousand Two Hundred Dollars ($14,200.00) to remedy all five of the defects described in Paragraphs 7 through 11. CAUSES OF ACTION

FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION — Breach of Contract

15. Plaintiff repeats and realleges paragraphs 1 through 14 as though fully set forth herein. The Contract dated November 4, 2025 is a valid, enforceable written agreement supported by consideration. Plaintiff performed all material obligations on his part, having paid $18,000.00 of $24,500.00 and having tendered access to the premises throughout the project. Defendants materially breached the Contract by, among other acts and omissions: failing to install cabinets level and plumb; installing a quartz countertop with a defective seam; installing porcelain floor tile that became loose and grout that cracked within weeks; failing to install a code-required GFCI outlet adjacent to the sink; failing to vent the range hood to the exterior; and abandoning the work site on January 22, 2026 prior to completion.

SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION — Breach of the Implied Warranty of Workmanlike Performance

16. Plaintiff repeats and realleges paragraphs 1 through 15 as though fully set forth herein. New York law implies into every home-improvement contract a warranty that the contractor will perform the work in a skillful and workmanlike manner. Defendants breached this implied warranty by performing the cabinet, countertop, tile, electrical, and ventilation work in a manner that fell below the standard of workmanship reasonably expected of a licensed New York City Home Improvement Contractor.

THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION — Violation of New York General Business Law § 349 (Deceptive Acts and Practices)

17. Plaintiff repeats and realleges paragraphs 1 through 16 as though fully set forth herein. Defendants engaged in deceptive acts and practices in the conduct of business, trade, or commerce in New York, in violation of General Business Law § 349, by, inter alia: representing that the work would conform to NYC Electrical and Mechanical Codes when Defendants knew or should have known that the work as performed did not so conform; representing that the quartz crack was the manufacturer's responsibility while concealing the role of seam preparation; and tendering an invoice for an alleged oral change order in violation of GBL § 771's writing requirement, the noncompliance with which is itself materially deceptive to a reasonable consumer.

FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION — Violation of NYC Administrative Code § 20-393 et seq. (Home Improvement Contractor Provisions)

18. Plaintiff repeats and realleges paragraphs 1 through 17 as though fully set forth herein. Defendants are subject to the obligations imposed on licensed Home Improvement Contractors by Title 20, Chapter 2, Subchapter 22 of the New York City Administrative Code, including but not limited to the requirements that contracts be in writing, that change orders be in writing, that work conform to applicable building and safety codes, and that contractors not abandon work without lawful cause. Defendants violated these provisions by, among other acts: invoicing for an oral change order in violation of the writing requirement; performing electrical and mechanical work in violation of the NYC Electrical Code and NYC Mechanical Code § 504; and abandoning the project on January 22, 2026 without lawful cause.

### I. Factual Background

On November 4, 2025, Mr. Park and Karras Custom Builders LLC executed a written home-improvement contract for the complete renovation of the kitchen at 1612 Argyle Road. The agreed total contract price was Twenty-Four Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($24,500), payable in three installments: a deposit of Eight Thousand Dollars ($8,000) at signing, a mid-project draw of Eight Thousand Dollars ($8,000), and a final payment of Eight Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($8,500) due upon completion. The contract specified a start date of December 1, 2025 and a substantial-completion date of January 15, 2026.

Mr. Park has paid Eighteen Thousand Dollars ($18,000) toward the contract — the November 4 deposit ($8,000) and the December 22, 2025 mid-project draw ($8,000) on schedule, plus an additional $2,000 advanced on January 6, 2026 to keep your subcontractors on the job after a delivery delay you attributed to the cabinet supplier. He has likewise refused, and properly refused, the $4,500 add-on invoice you tendered on January 15, 2026 styled as a mid-project change order for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet." That invoice is the subject of Section IV below.

On January 22, 2026, after a verbal exchange in the kitchen concerning the disputed $4,500 invoice, you and your crew left the job site. You have not returned. You have not communicated any schedule for return. You have not cured a single one of the defects identified in writing by Mr. Park's January 19, 2026 email, which you acknowledged receipt of by reply at 9:42 PM the same day. ### II. Itemized Defects

The following five defects have been documented by photograph, by Mr. Park's expense-and-condition spreadsheet (47 rows; tab titled "Kitchen Renovation 2025 - actual vs quoted"), and by the independent written estimate of Aldous Bremer of Bremer & Sons, 4128 18th Avenue, Brooklyn, dated February 12, 2026 (the "Bremer Estimate"):

**1. Cabinets installed off-level by 1/2 inch on the south wall run.** A four-foot level laid across the south-wall upper cabinet run reads a consistent half-inch deviation from horizontal at the right-hand terminus. This deviation is visible to the unaided eye, is documented by photographs IMG_0237 through IMG_0244, and exceeds any reasonable trade tolerance. The Architectural Woodwork Standards (AWI/AWMAC/WI, 2nd ed.) specify a maximum installation deviation of 1/8 inch over an eight-foot run for cabinet work at the "Custom" grade specified by the contract. One-half inch is four times that tolerance and is not "within trade tolerance" by any recognized standard.

**2. Quartz countertop cracked along the seam.** A through-thickness crack approximately eleven inches long has propagated along the mitered seam between the sink-run and return-run countertop slabs. The crack first became visible to Mr. Park on January 8, 2026, less than three weeks after install. The slabs were sourced from Crystallo Surfaces, batch QS-2025-1182. Mr. Park has been in direct contact with Crystallo Surfaces' warranty administrator, who has confirmed in writing that the cracking pattern is consistent with installation stress (insufficient mechanical support of the seam) rather than a product defect, and that warranty coverage in such circumstances rests with the installer, not the manufacturer. The Crystallo correspondence is preserved and will be produced in discovery.

**3. Approximately six (6) floor tiles loose; grout cracking in two areas.** Six porcelain floor tiles, located in the high-traffic zone between the refrigerator and the sink, return a hollow sound when tapped and rock under foot pressure, indicating inadequate thinset coverage. Grout cracking is visible in two distinct seams running parallel to the sink cabinet. These conditions are not "settling, normal in old buildings"; the Park residence is a brownstone with structural conditions long since stabilized, and the failures are localized to the area you tiled.

**4. Outlet next to sink not GFCI — NYC Electrical Code violation.** The duplex outlet installed approximately fourteen (14) inches to the right of the sink basin is a standard non-GFCI receptacle. This installation directly violates the New York City Electrical Code's incorporation of NEC §210.8, which requires GFCI protection for all 125-volt single-phase 15- and 20-ampere receptacles installed within six feet of the outside edge of a kitchen sink. This is not a discretionary upgrade or an "item to be discussed"; it is a code-mandated life-safety installation and was expressly included in the contract scope.

**5. Range hood vent not connected to exterior; vents into the upper cabinet.** The range hood you installed is presently exhausting cooking effluent, grease, and moisture into the interior of the upper cabinet directly above the range, rather than to the building exterior. This installation violates §504 of the New York City Mechanical Code (mechanical exhaust system termination requirements) and creates an active fire hazard from grease accumulation in an enclosed cabinet over a heat source. Your statement to Mr. Park that the exterior connection was "an item to be discussed with the electrician but never confirmed" is not credible: range-hood termination is a mechanical and not an electrical scope item, the exterior wall penetration was sketched on the contract scope-of-work rider you signed, and a registered NYC HIC contractor cannot leave an unvented hood in service without an explicit written waiver from the homeowner. None was given or requested.

### IV. Legal Theories

Mr. Park's claims rest on the following overlapping bases, each of which is independently sufficient to support recovery of the amount demanded below:

**(a) Breach of contract.** The November 4, 2025 contract obligated Karras Custom Builders LLC to substantially complete the scope by January 15, 2026 in a workmanlike manner. The work was neither substantially completed nor performed in a workmanlike manner. The walk-off on January 22, 2026 was a material breach.

**(b) Breach of the implied warranty of workmanlike performance.** New York recognizes an implied warranty that home-improvement work will be performed in a reasonably skillful and workmanlike manner. *Milos v. Renovax*, 187 A.D.3d 442 (1st Dep't 2020); *Gallagher v. KitchenWorks Corp.*, 152 Misc. 2d 211 (Civ. Ct. Kings Co. 2018). The defects above, individually and collectively, breach that warranty.

**(c) NY General Business Law §349 (deceptive acts and practices).** The marketing and sale of a home-improvement project by a licensed HIC, followed by performance that violates the very codes the license is conditioned upon, constitutes a deceptive practice within the meaning of GBL §349 and supports an award of statutory damages and attorney's fees in addition to actual damages.

**(d) NY General Business Law §771 (home-improvement contracts; written change-order requirement).** GBL §771 requires every home-improvement contract, and every change order modifying it, to be in writing and signed by the homeowner. Your purported $4,500 oral change order for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet" does not satisfy that requirement, was never reduced to writing, was never signed by Mr. Park, and is therefore unenforceable as a matter of New York law. Mr. Park's refusal to pay it cannot serve as a defense to your performance obligations or as the basis of a counterclaim.

**(e) NYC Administrative Code §20-393 et seq. and the NYC Electrical, Mechanical, and Building Codes.** As a licensed NYC Home Improvement Contractor (License #1374829), Karras Custom Builders LLC is bound by the substantive performance standards set forth in the NYC HIC licensing regime and by the building, electrical, and mechanical codes incorporated by reference. The non-GFCI outlet (Defect 4) and the unvented range hood (Defect 5) are independent code violations supporting both compensatory and, where appropriate, statutory recovery.
