## Question Presented

What licensing and consumer-protection statutes apply to Karras Custom Builders LLC's renovation contract, and how do they support Wendell Park's claim?

## Short Answer

Two statutory regimes converge in our favor. NYC Administrative Code §§20-385 through 20-410 — administered by the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) — requires every Home Improvement Contractor ("HIC") operating in the five boroughs to be licensed, to use written contracts, and to refrain from unfair or deceptive practices. New York General Business Law §771 layers on a state-wide writing requirement specific to home-improvement contracts and to any modification of such a contract. Read together, these provisions render Karras Custom Builders LLC's claimed oral $4,500 change order unenforceable as a matter of law, and they expose Karras to additional consumer-oriented liability under GBL §349 and NYC Admin Code §20-393. Karras IS licensed (HIC #1374829, verified active by Renee on 2026-02-12), so we proceed not on a "no-license" theory but on a violation-of-licensing-conduct-rules theory, which is the cleaner play in small-claims part anyway.

## Background

### NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection

The NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (formerly DCA, rebranded DCWP in 2020) administers HIC licensing. Any contractor performing residential improvement work over $200 within the City of New York must hold an active HIC license. Licensing requires a written examination, posting of a $20,000 surety bond, proof of general-liability insurance, and continuing compliance with consumer-protection rules codified at Title 6 of the Rules of the City of New York and at NYC Admin Code Title 20, Subchapter 22.

HIC license #1374829 is the operative license for our purposes. It is issued in the name of Karras Custom Builders LLC, with Stefan Karras listed as the principal. The license is presently active. The active status is confirmed (a) by direct query of the DCWP licensee-search portal on 2026-02-12 at 12:31 by Renee Choudhury, and (b) by parallel BBB lookup the same afternoon. Verification details appear in the appendix below.

### NY General Business Law §771

NY GBL §771 imposes mandatory written-contract and written-change-order requirements for all home-improvement contractors operating anywhere in the State of New York. The statute is consumer-protective in design and in interpretation; courts have repeatedly held that ambiguities are construed in the homeowner's favor and that compliance is a condition precedent to a contractor's recovery on a contract claim. The required elements of a §771 contract are:

(a) the contract must be in writing;
(b) it must be signed by both parties (homeowner and contractor);
(c) it must contain a description of the work to be performed and the materials to be supplied;
(d) it must include a payment schedule tied to the contract milestones;
(e) it must state estimated start and completion dates;
(f) it must identify any specific warranties extended by the contractor or by suppliers; and
(g) it must contain a notice of the homeowner's right to cancel.

The change-order requirement is particularly important to us. §771 expressly provides that any modification to a covered contract — including a modification to scope, materials, price, or schedule — must be in writing and signed by both parties. Oral modifications are unenforceable against the homeowner. Courts have not been receptive to "course-of-conduct" or "ratification" workarounds where the contractor's record-keeping is inadequate.

§771-a addresses the payment schedule itself: payments must correlate to actual work milestones and may not be front-loaded beyond the value of work delivered. §771-b establishes the homeowner's right of rescission within three business days of contract execution; failure to provide rescission notice extends the rescission window indefinitely under cases such as Frank v. DaimlerChrysler line of authority (analogized in the home-improvement context).

### NY General Business Law §349

GBL §349 is New York's general consumer-protection statute. It prohibits "deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any business, trade or commerce." Its three-part elements, as articulated by the Court of Appeals in Stutman v. Chemical Bank and refined in Oswego Laborers' Local 214 Pension Fund v. Marine Midland Bank, are: (1) the challenged conduct must be consumer-oriented; (2) the conduct must be materially misleading; and (3) the plaintiff must have suffered injury as a result. §349 is attractive procedurally because it provides for a $50 statutory minimum recovery, treble damages up to $1,000 in the court's discretion for willful violations, and reasonable attorney's fees — fee-shifting that is otherwise unavailable in small-claims part.

### NYC Admin Code §20-393

NYC Admin Code §20-393 is the conduct-prohibition section of the HIC licensing regime. It enumerates roughly two dozen prohibited acts, including engaging in "any fraudulent, deceptive or illegal practice"; abandoning or willfully failing to perform a contract without justification; misrepresenting product quality; failing to deliver promised materials; and demanding payment for work not performed. Remedies include consumer refunds, civil penalties, and license suspension or revocation through DCWP administrative process.

### NYC Admin Code §20-700 et seq. — Consumer Protection Law

NYC Admin Code §20-700 et seq. is New York City's broader Consumer Protection Law, layered on top of the HIC-specific provisions. It prohibits deceptive trade practices in consumer transactions and provides additional remedies, including a $500 statutory minimum per violation. While §349 is the headline state statute, §20-700 et seq. is sometimes more favorable in small-claims practice because the consumer-orientation analysis is more permissive.

## Analysis

### Application 1 — The base contract satisfies §771

The contract dated 2025-11-04, signed by Wendell Park and Stefan Karras, is in writing and contains substantially all of the §771 elements: scope (custom shaker-style maple cabinets, quartz countertops, porcelain floor tile, electrical updates including code-mandated GFCI outlets near sink), payment schedule ($8,000 deposit / $8,000 mid-project / $8,500 completion), estimated dates (start 2025-12-01; completion 2026-01-15), and signature lines for both parties. The contract document we have meets the §771 baseline. This is helpful: it means we are not arguing that Karras should be denied recovery under his counterclaim because his original contract was non-compliant. We are instead arguing the narrower point — that his claimed modification is non-compliant — which is a more credible posture before Judge Vega.

### Application 2 — The alleged $4,500 oral change order is unenforceable

This is our core statutory argument. Karras invoiced $4,500 on 2026-01-15 for what he describes as "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet" purportedly approved by Wendell verbally during the renovation. There is no written change order. There are no text messages, emails, photographs of a hand-signed addendum, or contemporaneous written acknowledgment. Wendell denies that he ever approved any modification to scope or price. Under GBL §771, oral approval — even if it occurred, which Wendell disputes — does not bind the homeowner. The change order is unenforceable as a matter of law. This disposes of Karras's counterclaim in its entirety on a clean statutory ground that does not require the court to weigh credibility.

### Application 3 — "Trade tolerance" defense does not save the cabinet-level claim

Karras asserts that the 1/2" off-level deviation on the south wall cabinet run is "within trade tolerance (1/4"–1/2")." Even taking that representation as factually accurate (which it is not — see below), trade tolerance is irrelevant to a workmanlike-performance claim if the deviation exceeds the recognized industry standard. The relevant published standard is NAHB Residential Construction Performance Guidelines, which sets the cabinet-installation tolerance at 1/4" in 32 inches of run. Wendell's measurements (corroborated by Aldous Bremer's 2026-02-12 estimate report) show 1/2" deviation. That is double the published tolerance. Karras's 1/4"–1/2" range is fabricated; he is conflating the wider tolerance for stud-wall framing (which is irrelevant once finished cabinetry is installed plumb-and-level) with finish-cabinet tolerance.

### Application 4 — Code violations support GBL §349 deception claim

The range hood vents into the cabinet above rather than to the exterior. This violates NYC Mechanical Code §504, which requires kitchen exhaust to discharge to the outdoors. The outlet next to the sink is not GFCI-protected, in violation of NEC 210.8(A)(7) as adopted in NYC Electrical Code. These are not subjective workmanship matters; they are Code violations. A licensed HIC who delivers Code-violating work and represents it as completed has engaged in materially misleading consumer-oriented conduct. Wendell relied on Karras's representation that the kitchen was complete (Karras invoiced for completion-tier payment) and suffered injury (must now pay Bremer & Sons $14,200 to remediate). This satisfies the three-part Oswego test for §349 liability.

### Application 5 — NYC Admin Code §20-393 gives us licensing-leverage

§20-393 specifically prohibits HIC engagement in "any fraudulent or deceptive practice." Code-violating work that is invoiced as completed work fits within the deceptive-practice rubric. The remedies under §20-393 — refund and license-suspension exposure — are administrative and not directly recoverable in our small-claims action, but they are useful settlement leverage. Felipe Ortega will understand that a final judgment establishing Code violations becomes evidence in any subsequent DCWP complaint, which Stefan Karras has every incentive to avoid.

### Application 6 — NYC Consumer Protection Law adds statutory-minimum cushion

NYC Admin Code §20-700 et seq. provides a $500 statutory minimum per violation. If the bench finds two or more discrete deceptive acts (for example: misrepresenting completion of the range-hood ventilation as one violation; misrepresenting GFCI compliance as another), the statutory floor scales accordingly. This is a fallback theory if our actual-damages calculation is challenged. We do not need to lead with it.

### Application 7 — Estoppel does not save Karras

Even if Karras testifies under oath that Wendell orally approved the $4,500 modification, the doctrine of equitable estoppel does not rescue him from §771's writing requirement. New York courts have consistently held that consumer-protection statutes such as §771 cannot be circumvented by an estoppel theory premised on the consumer's alleged conduct. The legislative purpose — to protect homeowners from exactly the kind of after-the-fact verbal-modification claim Karras is making — would be defeated. The leading authority is well-developed in the Second Department; KeyCite confirms current good law.

### Application 8 — Subcontractor and supplier issues do not absolve general contractor

Karras blames the cracked quartz countertop on Crystallo Surfaces (batch QS-2025-1182), framing the crack as a manufacturer-warranty problem. This argument fails on contract grounds. Wendell's contract is with Karras Custom Builders LLC, not with Crystallo. Under New York's workmanlike-performance standard and under the express terms of the Karras contract, Karras is the warrantor. If the slab failed because of installation stress (improper seam preparation, inadequate substrate support, or thermal cycling caused by the unconnected range hood venting heat into the cabinet), that is a Karras workmanship issue. If the slab failed because of material defect, Karras's remedy is against his supplier, not against the homeowner. The contractual flow-down does not run upward. Wendell may proceed against Karras for the entire countertop remediation cost as one component of damages.

### Application 9 — Prior complaints not character evidence but useful for impeachment

DCWP file shows two prior consumer complaints against Karras Custom Builders LLC, both resolved (one in 2022, one in 2023). Under FRE 404(a)/CPLR analog, prior complaints are not admissible to prove the propensity for misconduct in the present matter. However, if Karras testifies on direct that he is a "first-time defendant" or characterizes himself as having an "unblemished record," the door opens to impeachment with the DCWP file. We should be ready to make that argument and keep the certified DCWP printout in the exhibit binder, marked but not pre-offered.

### Bond claim possibility

The $20,000 surety bond on file is available to satisfy consumer claims where the contractor has been found liable and has not paid. Process: claim is filed directly with the surety carrier, accompanied by a copy of the judgment and a statement of the consumer's unsatisfied recovery. Bond proceeds are paid out to consumer-claimants in the order of judgment. Carmen's instruction: do not pursue the bond claim now; reserve as judgment-collection backstop if Karras fails to satisfy the small-claims judgment within thirty days of entry. Filing a bond claim prematurely tips Ortega off to our collection strategy and may also trigger a bond-call dispute that complicates collection without speeding it up.

### BBB record pull

A parallel pull of the Better Business Bureau record on 2026-02-12 confirmed two prior complaints (matching the DCWP file), both marked "resolved." BBB rating: B-. The B- rating is not a §349 violation by itself, but it corroborates a pattern. We will not lead with BBB material at the hearing — BBB is not a regulator and the bench will not weight it — but it is appropriate impeachment fodder if Karras claims a clean record.

## Practical Recommendations

1. Cite GBL §771 as the primary statutory hook in both the demand letter (06_demand-letter-2026-02-19.md) and at the hearing. The unenforceability of the oral change order disposes of the counterclaim cleanly and is easy to articulate to a small-claims bench.
2. Cite GBL §349 as the secondary hook, primarily for fee-shifting potential. Fee-shifting may motivate Ortega to recommend a higher settlement number once he sees the §349 prayer.
3. Cite NYC Admin Code §20-393 as enforcement-flavored authority in correspondence. Use it sparingly at the hearing — the bench is not the regulator and will not award DCWP-administrative remedies — but it sharpens the pressure narrative.
4. Reserve NYC Admin Code §20-700 et seq. as a fallback statutory-minimum theory if the actual-damages calculation is challenged.

## Practical Risks

A. §349 risk: §349 requires "consumer-oriented" conduct. Some Second Department cases have held that one-on-one transactions, particularly bespoke renovation contracts, are not "consumer-oriented" within the meaning of the statute. There is genuine doctrinal inconsistency here, and Carmen flags it. The countervailing line of authority (which we will rely on) holds that §349 reaches deceptive practices by licensed contractors in transactions with ordinary homeowners precisely because the licensing regime treats those homeowners as a protected consumer class. Both lines have current good law per KeyCite.

B. Jury risk: if the case were transferred out of small-claims part to civil court (it will not be — Wendell capped the demand at $7,500 specifically to anchor in small claims), a jury could find the oral change order valid despite §771. Juries are sometimes sympathetic to "we shook on it" testimony from contractors. The small-claims bench is a safer forum because Judge Vega will apply the statute. This is exactly why the cap-at-$7,500 strategy was chosen at intake.

## Conclusion

The licensing and consumer-protection landscape strongly favors Wendell. Karras is licensed and at risk of DCWP exposure if he loses on the merits. The oral $4,500 change order is unenforceable on its face under GBL §771; the counterclaim should fail. The Code violations (range hood, GFCI) supply independent §349 hooks. Our best statutory theory at the 2026-03-20 hearing will lead with §771 (clean, dispositive on the counterclaim), follow with §349 (deceptive non-conforming work), and reserve §20-393 / §20-700 as background pressure. We do not need to over-cite. Judge Vega's small-claims part runs on common-sense liability with statutory citations as backbone; we have both.

## Question Presented

What is the appropriate damages quantum to claim in Park v. Karras, and how should it be allocated for evidentiary presentation?

## Short Answer

Wendell Park's actual repair-cost damages, as quantified by the independent Bremer & Sons estimate dated 2026-02-12, total **$14,200**. We will, however, plead and prove damages of **$7,500** — the maximum permitted by the Kings County Civil Court Small Claims Part under N.Y. CCA §1801, and a number deliberately set at-or-near the small-claims cap. The election is not a concession on liability or on the existence of the larger loss; it is a procedural choice that (i) preserves Wendell's ability to obtain a final, enforceable judgment within roughly six weeks rather than the twelve-to-eighteen months a full civil-court action would require, (ii) keeps Wendell's out-of-pocket fee exposure at the flat $1,500 retainer rather than a multi-thousand-dollar civil-litigation engagement, (iii) honors Wendell's stated preference for finality over maximum theoretical recovery, and (iv) avoids the factfinder-discount and credibility risks attendant to presenting a $14,200 quantum to a non-expert tribunal. ## Election Analysis

### The Cap

N.Y. City Civil Court Act §1801 caps small-claims jurisdiction at **$10,000** (exclusive of interest and disbursements). We are not pleading at the cap; we are pleading at $7,500.

### The Forbearance Math

- Actual damages (Bremer estimate): **$14,200**
- Claim filed: **$7,500**
- Voluntary forbearance: **$6,700** ($14,200 − $7,500)

Wendell is voluntarily forgoing $6,700 of facially recoverable damages in exchange for the procedural advantages described below. That forbearance is not a concession that the larger number is wrong; it is a litigation-economics decision.

### Rationale for Election

(a) **Speed.** Small-claims part offers a first hearing within roughly six weeks of intake (Mon 2026-02-09 → Fri 2026-03-20). A civil-court action under CPLR Article 30 would, on Kings County's current calendar, take twelve to eighteen months to first dispositive event.

(b) **Cost.** Our retainer is a flat $1,500 plus the $20 filing fee. A civil-court engagement on the same facts would carry hourly billing in the $4,000–$8,000 range through trial. The cost differential alone consumes a meaningful share of the $6,700 we are forgoing.

(c) **Wendell's stated preference for finality.** Wendell told me at intake (2026-02-09) and confirmed at retainer signing (2026-02-11) that he prefers a quick, certain resolution over a maximized but delayed recovery. He used the phrase "I want this closed before the spring."

(d) **Jury risk avoided.** Small-claims part is a bench proceeding before a single judicial officer (here Hon. Marisol Vega, Part 5). There is no jury, no voir dire, and no risk of an outlier verdict either above or below the cap.

### Documentation of the Forbearance

The voluntary forbearance is papered in two places: (i) **Article 6 of the retainer**, which expressly recites that the Client has elected to limit the claim to $7,500 with the understanding that any portion above the cap is not recoverable in this proceeding; and (ii) a one-page **written informed-consent disclosure** Wendell signed on 2026-02-11, confirming that he was advised of the civil-court alternative, of the approximate cost and timeline of that alternative, and of the right to ask additional questions. This dual papering is intended to foreclose any post-hoc claim that Wendell did not understand what he was electing.

### Collateral Preservation

Election to file in small-claims does not waive collateral remedies. In particular, the **HIC Home Improvement Contractor bond** posted by Karras under NYC Admin Code §20-394 et seq. — bond amount **$20,000** — remains available as a separate collection vehicle for any uncollected portion of a judgment, and (subject to bond-claim procedures and notice requirements) for any portion of the loss that exceeds the $7,500 awarded here. The bond claim is a parallel administrative remedy and is not foreclosed by the small-claims judgment so long as the small-claims pleading does not release Karras for amounts beyond the pleaded sum (it does not). I have confirmed bond status with the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on 2026-02-13 (DCWP file note in matter folder).

### Civil-Court Alternative — Why Not

A civil-court (CPLR Article 30) action on the same operative facts would seek:

- **Principal.** Full $14,200 actual damages.
- **Statutory adders.** GBL §349(h) attorney's fees, NYC Admin Code §20-700 statutory damages.
- **Pre-judgment interest.** CPLR §5001(a) at the 9% statutory rate.

Theoretical ceiling on a civil-court verdict approaches $20,000–$24,000. Against that, however, we estimate: 12+ months to first dispositive event; $4,000–$8,000 in additional fees on an hourly engagement; meaningful expert-disclosure exposure (Wendell would likely need a paid construction expert, not just a fact-witness contractor); jury risk in either direction. On Wendell's stated preferences, the civil-court route is dominated by the small-claims route.

## Fee-Shifting Analysis

The pleadings will request — without overstating prospects — every fee-shifting and statutory-adder hook the facts support, while frankly acknowledging that small-claims part historically awards these sparingly.

- **GBL §349(h) — Deceptive Acts and Practices.** Section 349 provides for **actual damages**, **$50 per-violation statutory damages**, and **reasonable attorney's fees** if plaintiff prevails on a §349 claim. In small-claims part, fee awards are rare but available; my realistic working range is **$850–$1,500**, scaled to the flat $1,500 retainer. We will request fees in the complaint and will support the request at hearing with a one-page affidavit of services.

- **NYC Admin Code §20-700 — Consumer Protection Law.** §20-700 provides a statutory-damages floor of **$500 per violation**. Across the five defects (cabinets, countertop, floor, GFCI, range hood) that line could potentially add **$2,500** (5 × $500). The §20-700 adder is, however, capped by the overall **$10,000** small-claims jurisdictional limit and by the principle that statutory damages cannot duplicate compensatory recovery for the same conduct.

- **§349 statutory floor.** §349 itself provides only **$50 per consumer violation** as statutory damages, plus actual damages and fees. The $50/violation figure is symbolic in the context of a $7,500 claim but is worth pleading because it preserves the §349 claim as a fee-shifting hook.

### Recovery Breakdown — If Successful

| Component | Amount |
|---|---|
| Principal claim (capped) | $7,500 |
| Filing-fee reimbursement (CCA §1804) | $20 |
| §349 attorney-fee request (working figure) | $850 |
| **Ceiling — pleaded recovery** | **$8,370** |

We will not promise Wendell any specific recovery; the retainer's Article 6 informed-consent recital is explicit on that point.

## Counterclaim Offset Analysis

Karras's Answer (served 2026-03-03 by Felipe Ortega) raises a counterclaim of **$4,500** for the alleged mid-project change order. If Hon. Vega credits the counterclaim in full, net recovery would be reduced to roughly **$3,000** ($7,500 − $4,500). Mitigation:

A purely verbal $4,500 change order is **unenforceable** under §771 against the consumer. I will move at hearing to dismiss the counterclaim on this ground; if Hon. Vega declines to dismiss outright, §771 still substantially weights the credibility analysis in Wendell's favor.
- **Karras's documentary record.** Karras has refused to produce text messages from the relevant period (Carmen flagged for meet-and-confer on 2026-03-12). The absence of any written confirmation reinforces the §771 attack.

Best-case offset is therefore $0 (counterclaim dismissed); worst-credible offset is partial. I assess expected offset at $0–$1,500.

- **Carmen's counter.** $7,000.
- **Walk-away.** Below $5,000 we proceed to hearing on 2026-03-20.

## Risks

- **Risk of undervaluing.** Hon. Vega could discount Aldous's estimate as an "advocate's number." Mitigation: Aldous is an independent licensed contractor with no fee paid for the estimate and no other financial relationship with Wendell or with our office; the comparative-quote sheet places Aldous's $14,200 at the median of three independent estimates. The forbearance to $7,500 is itself a hedge against discount: even a 50% haircut on the underlying $14,200 still leaves the $7,500 claim fully supported.

**$7,500 is the right number.** It is the small-claims-part ceiling, it represents approximately 53% of the $14,200 independently quantified actual damages, and the voluntary forbearance is fully papered in retainer Article 6 and in Wendell's signed informed-consent disclosure. ## Question Presented

What procedural rules govern the Park v. Karras small-claims action, and what strategic implications follow for venue, evidence, and remedy?

## Short Answer

The action is properly brought in the Small Claims Part of NYC Civil Court under New York City Civil Court Act ("CCA") §§1801–1814. The Part has a money-only jurisdictional cap of $10,000; trial is to the bench under a relaxed "substantial justice" evidentiary standard; filing is by sworn statement on a $20 fee; and appeal is narrowly limited to whether substantial justice has been done. The forum is fast (typical 4–8 weeks to first hearing; here ~3.5 weeks), cheap, and informal — well-matched to Wendell Park's $7,500 claim. The trade-offs are real: (i) Wendell forecloses any recovery above the elected $7,500 in this forum, even though Aldous Bremer's repair estimate is $14,200; (ii) the defendant retains a §1806 jury-demand option that could remove the matter to the regular Civil Part for jury trial (low risk on these facts but not zero); and (iii) discovery is by leave only, making strategic use of the §1804 informal-evidence rule and adverse-inference doctrine load-bearing. On balance, election of small-claims is sound. Settlement floor: $5,000.

## Background

The Park v. Karras matter is a homeowner-versus-contractor defect case arising from a $24,500 kitchen renovation contract signed 2025-11-04 between Wendell Park (homeowner, 1612 Argyle Road, Brooklyn) and Stefan Karras d/b/a Karras Custom Builders LLC (NYC HIC license #1374829). Wendell paid $18,000; Karras walked off on 2026-01-22 after a dispute over a $4,500 change-order invoice that Wendell rejected. Five enumerated defects (off-level cabinets, cracked quartz seam, loose floor tile, non-GFCI sink-adjacent outlet, range hood vented to a cabinet). Bremer & Sons issued a written repair estimate of $14,200 on 2026-02-12. We elected to file at $7,500 — at-or-near the $10,000 statutory cap — to retain small-claims venue.

Filing occurred 2026-02-26 in Kings County Civil Court, Small Claims Part, 141 Livingston Street, Brooklyn NY 11201; index SC-002847-26/KI; assigned to Hon. Marisol Vega, Part 5; first hearing Friday 2026-03-20 at 9:30 AM. Filing fee $20 paid by money order. Clerk of intake: Rosalind Imhotep.

This memo collects the procedural framework, with strategic notes drawn from three prior appearances by the undersigned before Hon. Vega (consumer-loan defense 2024-04; landlord deposit 2024-11; cell-carrier billing 2025-06).

## Analysis

### 1. Statutory framework — CCA §§1801–1814

The Small Claims Part is a creature of statute. The operative provisions are:

- **§1801 — Definition and cap.** Defines "small claim" as any cause of action *for money only*, not exceeding $10,000, brought by a *natural person*. Equitable relief, replevin, specific performance, and declaratory judgment are unavailable. Wendell's $7,500 demand, sounding in breach of contract / consequential damages for defective workmanship, is a paradigmatic money-only claim.

- **§1802 — Venue.** Proper in the county where the defendant resides, has an office for the transaction of business, or where a regular employment is maintained. Karras resides in Bay Ridge (Kings County) and operates Karras Custom Builders LLC out of a Kings County address; venue in Kings County is proper on multiple grounds.

- **§1803 — Procedure for commencement.** Action initiated by the plaintiff (or someone duly authorized) appearing at the clerk's office, filing a sworn or verified statement of claim, and paying the nominal filing fee. The clerk causes notice to be served on the defendant by ordinary first-class and certified mail at the defendant's residence or business. Service is administrative — no plaintiff-side process server required.

- **§1804 — Informal hearing.** *Hearings shall be conducted in such form and manner as to do substantial justice between the parties according to the rules of substantive law.* The formal rules of evidence and pleading do not apply except those concerning privileged communications. **Hearsay is receivable** but is to be weighed by the trier of fact "according to its probative value." This is the most consequential rule for our case: it lets us put Margot Lévesque's percipient observations and Aldous Bremer's written estimate before the court without strict CPLR-Article-45 foundations.

- **§1805 — Bench trial.** Trial is to the court without a jury, except as provided in §1806.

- **§1806 — Defendant's jury option.** *The defendant* may demand a jury trial on payment of a $70 jury fee plus posting an undertaking, in which event the matter is removed to the regular Civil Part. Plaintiff has no jury right. (See §2 below for strategic discussion.)

- **§1807 — Limited appeal.** Either party may appeal to the Appellate Term of the Supreme Court within 30 days, but the standard of review is whether *substantial justice* has been done according to the rules of substantive law — *Hill v. Arnold*, 226 N.Y.S.2d 84 (App. Term 1st Dep't 1962) and progeny. This is a narrow review; reversal is exceptional. The narrow appellate window cuts both ways: it caps Karras's downside-deferral options if we win, but it likewise caps our review options if we lose.

- **§1808 — Limited res judicata.** A small-claims judgment is res judicata only as to the amount adjudged. It does *not* preclude relitigation of the same issue in a subsequent action between the same parties, except as to that amount. Practical implication: Wendell theoretically retains a separate civil action for the $6,700 differential ($14,200 − $7,500), though the practical and equitable barriers to such a follow-on suit are formidable, and Carmen will counsel Wendell that the small-claims judgment functionally ends the matter.

- **§1809 — Plaintiff must be a natural person.** Corporations, partnerships, associations, assignees, and insurers may not maintain a small-claims action in this Part — they are routed to the *Commercial Claims* Part (§§1801-A et seq.). Wendell sues in his individual capacity as homeowner; he qualifies.

- **§1812-A — Costs and disbursements.** Costs are recoverable but **attorneys' fees generally are not, absent statutory authorization**. Possible fee-shifting hooks worth flagging: NY General Business Law §349 (deceptive acts and practices) and §771 (Home Improvement Business — written contract, deposit limits, escrow) do contain attorney-fee provisions in narrow circumstances. We should evaluate a §349/§771 angle separately (see 19_contractor-licensing-research.md), but I do not plan to plead those theories in the small-claims forum because (i) §1801's "money only" framing complicates the equitable predicates, and (ii) preserving doctrinal cleanliness matters in front of Hon. Vega.

- **§1813 — Enforcement.** Judgments enforceable as in any civil action; transcript may be filed in Supreme Court for docketing as a money judgment.

- **§1814 — Effect.** Statute is to be liberally construed.

Collateral: **CPLR 4547** (settlement-communication privilege) applies in small-claims as in any civil proceeding; statements made in the 2026-03-13 Ortega/Wendell settlement exchange ($3,200 offer) are inadmissible to prove liability or amount. We will not reference the offer at the hearing absent a §4547(a) impeachment hook.

### 2. Election strategy — the $7,500 / $10,000 question

Wendell's repair damages, as established by Bremer's 2026-02-12 estimate, are $14,200. By filing at $7,500 we (i) keep the matter in the Small Claims Part (under the $10,000 cap and well clear of any §1806 defendant-driven removal incentive), and (ii) waive the $6,700 excess in this forum. A subsequent civil-court action for that excess is theoretically available under §1808's limited res judicata rule but is practically foreclosed by issue preclusion on liability findings, by Wendell's expressed preference to "be done with this guy," and by the cost asymmetry of a second lawsuit.

Carmen documents Wendell's *informed consent* to the election in the 2026-02-09 intake notes and the 2026-02-11 retainer. The retainer itself (¶7) recites the election, the cap, and the waiver of the excess. (See 02_retainer-agreement.md and 04_case-strategy-initial-memo.md.)

Why $7,500 and not $9,999.99? Because we want headroom for (i) Hon. Vega's customary practice of awarding modestly under the demand when the demand is at-cap (the "credibility tax" pattern observed across the three prior appearances), and (ii) signaling reasonable restraint to a judge who is, in my experience, allergic to plaintiffs who appear to be gaming the cap.

### 3. Defendant's §1806 jury demand — risk assessment

§1806 permits the *defendant* to demand a jury trial, removing the matter to the regular Civil Court Part. The mechanics: $70 jury fee plus an undertaking (typically $50) plus a verified statement specifying issues of fact triable by jury. Filing must occur within five days of receipt of the notice of claim (§1806).

For Karras, the cost-benefit math weighs heavily against demand:
- His counterclaim is $4,500 — sub-cap and modestly sized.
- A jury trial in the regular Civil Part would pull him into CPLR Article 31 discovery, exposing his text messages (which on our preliminary signal he is reluctant to produce — see 23_discovery-responses-received.md), his prior-complaint history, and his communications with Crystallo Surfaces.
- Felipe Ortega is a sole practitioner; the marginal billable hours for a jury trial materially exceed those for a small-claims hearing, raising Karras's defense cost.
- The five-day window has run; absent leave for a late demand, the option is functionally extinguished as of 2026-03-04.

I assess the §1806 transfer risk at *very low*. We should not modify our trial preparation around it.

### 4. Discovery limits — informal regime

Small-claims is an informal forum. **CPLR Article 31 does not strictly apply**; there is no presumptive right to depositions, interrogatories, or document demands. The court tolerates limited document requests by leave on a showing of necessity and proportionality, and informal requests by counsel are common where both sides are represented.

Our 2026-03-05 discovery service (5 interrogatories + targeted document requests including text-message production for the period 2025-11-04 through 2026-01-22) is on the upper end of what Hon. Vega's part will tolerate but well within practice. Ortega's 2026-03-12 responses produced documents but refused the text-message production. Carmen has flagged a meet-and-confer.

**Adverse-inference instruction.** §1804's substantial-justice principle empowers the court, in its discretion, to draw an adverse inference where a party has failed to produce relevant non-privileged evidence within its control. There is no formal CPLR 3126 sanctions framework available, but the substantive doctrine is the same. Our hearing strategy includes a concise oral motion for adverse inference re: the text messages, framed under §1804 and the substantial-justice standard. (See 28_hearing-prep-outline.md.)

### 5. Witness procedure

Parties may bring witnesses informally — no subpoena required where the witness appears voluntarily. Subpoenas (subpoena ad testificandum and subpoena duces tecum) are available on application to the clerk; witness fees are statutory ($15/day plus $0.23/mile). Margot Lévesque has agreed to attend voluntarily; Aldous Bremer is on standby and we will subpoena duces tecum only if Ortega challenges the estimate's authenticity.

### 6. Evidence admissibility

Under §1804:
- **Written estimates** from contractors are routinely admissible without live testimony when authenticated by the party who received them (here, Wendell). Bremer's $14,200 estimate on Bremer & Sons letterhead can come in through Wendell's foundation testimony; Bremer's live appearance provides corroboration but is not strictly required.
- **Photographs** are admissible with witness foundation — Wendell took ~60 phone photos; we will narrow to 12 for the exhibit binder (item 31, Practical Recommendations).
- **Hearsay** is receivable but weighted by the court. Margot's account of the two arguments she observed through the open kitchen window is partly hearsay (Karras's statements are admissions, non-hearsay; Wendell's are arguably prior consistent statements); we present without objection.
- **The contract and change-order communications** are documents in the parties' possession and present no admissibility issue.
- **Karras's "Crystallo Surfaces batch QS-2025-1182" warranty defense** is hearsay but admissible under §1804; we rebut by pointing to installation rather than manufacture as the seam-crack mechanism.

### 7. Settlement at hearing

## III. Case Digests

### Case 1 — *Milos v. Renovax, Inc.*, 187 AD3d 442 (1st Dep't 2020)

**Citation:** *Milos v. Renovax, Inc.*, 187 AD3d 442, 132 NYS3d 18 (1st Dep't 2020).

**Court / Year:** Appellate Division, First Department, 2020. Decision below: Sup. Ct. New York County, 2019.

**Holding:** A purported oral mid-project change order in a residential home-improvement contract is unenforceable against the consumer under GBL §771, which requires home-improvement contracts and material modifications to be in writing and signed. The contractor is barred from collecting on the unwritten modification and may not assert it as a counterclaim or offset.

**Reasoning:** GBL §771 is consumer-protective and strictly construed against the contractor. The court rejected verbal "go-ahead" plus partial performance as ratification, holding the writing requirement is substantive, not evidentiary. Allowing oral modifications to slip past §771 invites the very abuse the statute prevents. Quantum-meruit fallback was rejected because the labor and materials fell within the original written scope.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Directly supports rejection of Karras's $4,500 counterclaim for "upgraded cabinet hardware and additional outlet." No signed change order exists; Karras's sole evidence is a self-serving statement that Wendell "verbally approved." *Milos* forecloses the counterclaim and defeats the quantum-meruit retreat Ortega is likely to attempt. I lead the §771 portion of the hearing with this case.

### Case 2 — *Gallagher v. KitchenWorks Corp.*, 152 Misc 2d 211 (Civ Ct Kings Co. 2018)

**Citation:** *Gallagher v. KitchenWorks Corp.*, 152 Misc 2d 211, 89 NYS3d 614 (Civ Ct Kings Co. 2018).

**Court / Year:** Civil Court of the City of New York, Kings County, 2018. Bench trial decision by Hon. R. Acheampong.

**Holding:** Cabinet installation that exceeds professional trade tolerances — there, a 3/8" deviation across a 9-foot run — constitutes breach of the implied warranty of workmanlike performance. The contractor's argument that "trade tolerance" excuses any deviation up to 1/2" was rejected as inconsistent with NKBA installation standards and with the parties' written specification.

**Reasoning:** The implied warranty of workmanlike performance is a freestanding obligation independent of express contract terms. A contractor who holds himself out as skilled in cabinetry implicitly warrants installation to professional standards. The "trade tolerance" defense was characterized as the contractor unilaterally lowering the standard of care; the proper benchmark is industry consensus.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Supports Defect 1 (cabinets installed off-level by 1/2 inch on the south wall run). Karras's anticipated defense — "within trade tolerance (1/4" – 1/2")" — is exactly what *Gallagher* rejected. Our 1/2" deviation is at the upper edge of Karras's claimed range and outside any NKBA standard I can locate. Useful that *Gallagher* is from this very court (Kings County Civil Court), which Hon. Vega is likely to weight heavily.

### Case 3 — *Persaud v. NYC Refit LLC*, 2019 NY Slip Op 50217(U) (Civ Ct Queens Co. 2019)

**Citation:** *Persaud v. NYC Refit LLC*, 63 Misc 3d 1216(A), 2019 NY Slip Op 50217(U) (Civ Ct Queens Co. 2019) (table).

**Court / Year:** Civil Court, Queens County, 2019. Hon. T. Adamopoulos.

**Holding:** A contractor's failure to vent a range hood to the building exterior — instead venting into an adjacent cabinet cavity — violates NYC Mechanical Code §§ MC 401.4 and MC 504 and supports a refund of the labor and materials allocated to the range-hood installation, plus consequential damages for the cost of cure.

**Reasoning:** Compliance with the NYC Mechanical Code is a baseline implied term of any residential kitchen-renovation contract; venting grease-laden air into joinery is a code violation, not a design choice. The contractor's "intended to discuss with the HVAC sub" line did not excuse the violation, because the obligation to the homeowner is not delegable.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Supports Defect 5 (range hood vent not connected to exterior; vents into the cabinet above). Karras's "item to be discussed with electrician but never confirmed by Wendell" defense maps one-to-one onto the failed defense in *Persaud*. I plan to mark *Persaud* as Exhibit-Tab L.

### Case 4 — *Schein v. Powerplay Builders, LLC*, 178 AD3d 1102 (2d Dep't 2019)

**Citation:** *Schein v. Powerplay Builders, LLC*, 178 AD3d 1102, 116 NYS3d 296 (2d Dep't 2019).

**Court / Year:** Appellate Division, Second Department, 2019. On appeal from the Appellate Term, 9th & 10th Judicial Districts.

**Holding:** The "substantial justice" standard governing small-claims proceedings under N.Y. City Civil Court Act §1804 authorizes the court to give an adverse-inference instruction (or, in a bench trial, to draw an adverse inference) where a party refuses to produce contemporaneous text messages after receiving a preservation notice and informal document request, and offers no credible explanation for the refusal.

**Reasoning:** Small-claims practice is flexible; strict CPLR spoliation compliance is not required for an adverse inference. What is required: (i) some preservation request or notice, (ii) the responding party's apparent control of the missing material, and (iii) a record that the refusal is not innocently explained. The substantial-justice standard cuts both ways and is not a license to stonewall.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Supports my adverse-inference request on Karras's text-message refusal. On 2026-03-12, Ortega's discovery responses confirmed Karras would not produce texts from the relevant period (December 2025 through 2026-01-22). My 03-05 informal document request expressly named texts; the 02-19 demand letter served as a litigation-hold notice. I will request the inference orally and have a one-page *Schein* excerpt ready for the bench.

### Case 5 — *Oswald v. Brooklyn Granite Co.*, 28 Misc 3d 1206(A) (Civ Ct Kings Co. 2010)

**Citation:** *Oswald v. Brooklyn Granite Co.*, 28 Misc 3d 1206(A), 2010 NY Slip Op 51184(U) (Civ Ct Kings Co. 2010).

**Court / Year:** Civil Court, Kings County, 2010. Hon. P. Velasquez.

**Holding:** A countertop seam crack within thirty days of installation is a workmanship issue, not a materials defect, regardless of any supplier's manufacturer warranty. The installing contractor cannot delegate workmanship to the slab fabricator and remains liable for cost of cure.

**Reasoning:** A doctrinal line separates materials defects (supplier warranty) from workmanship defects (contractor's implied warranty). The homeowner's privity is with the contractor; the contractor takes on the risk of fabrication and seam quality at the moment he accepts and installs the slab. Seam failure within thirty days is presumptively workmanship — inadequate adhesive, mismatched substrate, or improper support across the seam — absent affirmative evidence otherwise.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Rebuts Karras's "Crystallo Surfaces, batch QS-2025-1182, manufacturer warranty" defense for Defect 2 (countertop cracked along the seam within three weeks of install; visible 2026-01-08). Three weeks sits well inside the thirty-day workmanship presumption. Karras has produced no fabrication-defect documentation from Crystallo; he has only redirected.

### Case 6 — *Doroshow v. New York Tile Inc.*, 2017 NY Slip Op 50312(U) (Civ Ct Bronx Co. 2017)

**Citation:** *Doroshow v. New York Tile Inc.*, 55 Misc 3d 1208(A), 2017 NY Slip Op 50312(U) (Civ Ct Bronx Co. 2017) (table).

**Court / Year:** Civil Court, Bronx County, 2017. Hon. F. Mariotta.

**Holding:** Floor-tile loosening within weeks of installation is attributable to improper subfloor preparation, inadequate thinset coverage, or improper grout joints — not to "settling" of an old building. "Settling" is a generalized excuse that requires expert support to be credited; the default inference, particularly within an early post-installation window, is workmanship failure.

**Reasoning:** The court canvassed TCNA Handbook and ANSI A108 standards and held that a properly prepped subfloor with adequate thinset coverage tolerates ordinary structural movement in pre-war housing. Tiles loosening within weeks more probably indicate sub-100% thinset coverage or substrate moisture — both workmanship issues. "Settling" was rejected as conclusory.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Rebuts Karras's "settling, normal in old buildings" defense for Defect 3 (~6 floor tiles loose; grout cracking in two areas). Wendell's brownstone is genuinely old, so the defense has surface plausibility — but *Doroshow* is exactly the case for puncturing it. Bremer's estimate notes "thinset coverage appears inadequate; grout joints under-spec'd," which dovetails.

### Case 7 — *Karpenko v. Bayside Electric Corp.*, 162 AD3d 994 (2d Dep't 2018)

**Citation:** *Karpenko v. Bayside Electric Corp.*, 162 AD3d 994, 79 NYS3d 268 (2d Dep't 2018).

**Court / Year:** Appellate Division, Second Department, 2018.

**Holding:** The NYC Electrical Code's GFCI requirement for receptacles within six feet of a sink (NYC Electrical Code §210.8) is a non-delegable duty. The general contractor remains liable for code violations regardless of whether the work was performed directly or through an electrical subcontractor.

**Reasoning:** Life-safety obligations cannot be shifted to subcontractors by contractual arrangement. The general contractor pulls (or fails to pull) the permit and delivers the finished product to the homeowner. "I told the electrician" is irrelevant to the homeowner's claim, though it may matter for GC-sub indemnification.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Supports Defect 4 (outlet next to sink not GFCI). Karras's contract scope explicitly listed "electrical updates including code-mandated GFCI outlets near sink." Any redirection to an unnamed electrical sub does not matter for our claim. Particularly useful because Second Department is binding on Hon. Vega.

### Case 8 — *Velasquez v. Avant Garde Renovation Group*, 192 AD3d 705 (2d Dep't 2021)

**Citation:** *Velasquez v. Avant Garde Renovation Group*, 192 AD3d 705, 144 NYS3d 218 (2d Dep't 2021).

**Court / Year:** Appellate Division, Second Department, 2021.

**Holding:** GBL §349 (deceptive acts and practices) applies to consumer-oriented home-improvement transactions where the contractor's conduct is materially misleading and has broad impact on consumers, not merely on the individual homeowner. Statutory attorney's fees under §349(h) are recoverable in the small-claims part of the New York City Civil Court, subject to the small-claims monetary cap on the principal recovery; fees are awarded outside the cap.

**Reasoning:** §349 is not unavailable in small claims by reason of informal procedure. The "consumer-oriented" element is satisfied by standardized practice — uniform contract language, repeated billing patterns across customers — not by any single transaction. Fee-shifting is remedial and tracks the principal recovery without being capped by it.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Supports a §349 cause of action alongside breach of contract, and a fee-shifting request if §349 is sustained. Karras's HIC license is intact, but his pattern — verbal "change orders" in round-number amounts, vague defenses ("trade tolerance," "settling"), abandonment after disputed invoices — has the shape of a consumer-oriented practice. Two prior BBB complaints (both resolved) are not strong pattern evidence, so §349 stays secondary rather than lead.

### Case 9 (held in reserve) — *Reyes v. Empire Renovation Group*, 2022 NY Slip Op 50421(U) (Civ Ct Bronx Co. 2022)

**Citation:** *Reyes v. Empire Renovation Group*, 75 Misc 3d 1217(A), 2022 NY Slip Op 50421(U) (Civ Ct Bronx Co. 2022) (table).

**Court / Year:** Civil Court, Bronx County, 2022.

**Holding:** A contractor's BBB record (including resolved complaints) is generally inadmissible as character evidence in the homeowner's case-in-chief. It becomes admissible for impeachment if and only if the contractor takes the stand and asserts a clean track record or a specific count of satisfied customers, opening the door under Rule 608-style impeachment principles as adapted to civil practice.

**Reasoning:** Prejudice-versus-probativity calculus plus the rule against general bad-act evidence. The mere filing of a BBB complaint says little about the present claim's merits and risks confusing the trier of fact.

**Application to *Park v. Karras*:** Confirms my strategy of **not** introducing Karras's two BBB complaints affirmatively in the case-in-chief. If Karras takes the stand and characterizes himself as a clean operator, *Reyes* is loaded for impeachment. Hearing-day judgment call.

CONSERVATION TIP OF THE MONTH
----------------------------------------------------------------

  =E2=98=85 Bleed your radiators: Trapped air in steam radiators reduces
    efficiency. Bleeding takes 5 minutes and can save up to 10% on heating
    bills.

If your apartment has cast=2Diron steam radiators (very common in pre=2Dwa=
r
Brooklyn buildings), trapped air pockets at the top of the radiator prevent
hot steam from filling the full body of the unit. The result: the bottom
half is scalding and the top half stays cool, the radiator clangs and bangs
("water hammer"), and your boiler runs longer to compensate. Bleeding is
the process of opening the small valve on the side of the radiator with a
radiator key (a square=2Ddrive key, available at any hardware store for $3)
and letting the trapped air hiss out until a small bead of water appears.
Then close the valve. Total time: about five minutes per radiator. If your
radiator clangs at night when the heat first comes on, this is almost
certainly your fix. If clanging persists after bleeding, the radiator may
not be properly pitched toward the supply pipe =E2=80=94 ask your building
super to check the level.

# 287 Lincoln Place, Apt 3B — Bills Summary, October 2025

Compiled by Yael Strauss, 2025-10-31 23:40 (after the Halloween thing). Reviewed by Wren Calderón, 2025-11-01 10:11.

Reference period: 2025-10-01 → 2025-10-31.

---

## Executive line

Net: Wren owes Yael **$5.95** as of 11-01 (Halloween settlement). All other items settled in-month.

---

## Section 1 — Rent

### 1.1 Payment

$3,400, split 50/50, $1,700 each. Wren's half was covered by Yael on 09-30 22:14 (payroll glitch); Wren paid Yael back $1,700 via Zelle on 10-03 09:42. Both Zelle confirmations live in `house/bills/rent-receipt-october.eml` along with Esra's "received, thanks" line.

The only money tension we had this period; resolved within 72 hours. Logged here for completeness, not as a recurring concern. The amended house rules (10-12) now codify a "if payroll slips, the covering roommate is paid back within 7 calendar days, no interest, no penalty" clause — a small after-the-fact piece of bookkeeping that we both signed off on. Cross-ref `house/rules/house-rules-amended-2025-10-12.md`, §4.

### 1.2 Note

I (Yael) want to flag that the rent dispute, such as it was, was brief. Wren apologized in person and again over coffee at Sey on 10-04. It does not need to keep showing up in these summaries beyond October. As of November 1, the books are clean.

---

## Section 2 — Utilities

### 2.1 ConEd electric (account in Yael's name)

October invoice — **$96.71** (cycle 2025-09-04 → 2025-10-03). Up-tick because heating started early evenings; the apartment runs the steam heat from the boiler, but the thermostat-driven supplemental electric kicks in before the radiators come on, which seems to be where the extra ~$12 over September lives. Wren's share $48.355 → rounded **$48.36**.

Status: Wren Venmo'd $48.36 on 10-06, memo "con ed oct ⚡". Settled.

Cross-ref: see `house/bills/conded-october.eml`.

(October's gas bill made me start thinking of the radiator as a small extortionate roommate.)

The cycle-vs-billing-period thing keeps tripping me up: ConEd's "service period" is 2025-09-04 → 2025-10-03 (30 days), but the "billing period" listed on the PDF top-line is 2025-10-04 → 2025-11-03, which is the window inside which the bill is due. Both labels are reproduced in the .eml. I'm noting it here so future-me does not, again, write a frantic 10:30 PM message to Wren saying "wait, did we already pay this." We did. We always have.

### 2.2 National Grid gas (account in Wren's name)

October invoice — **$58.83** (≈2.6× Sept's $22.40). Yael's share **$29.42** (rounded from $29.415). The jump is the boiler. Once the building flips into heating-season mode the gas usage goes up sharply because the boiler is shared but the apartments split out via sub-meter; ours seems to be on the higher side of the building average, which Joaquín explained is partly because 3B is a corner unit with two exterior walls.

Status: Yael Venmo'd $29.42 on 10-09, memo "national grid oct". Settled.

Cross-ref: see `national-grid-october.eml`.

Note: Heat was on for cycles after sundown all month. Thermostat 67°F default. We agreed informally (over chiles en nogada on 10-26) to keep it at 67 through November and revisit in December if it gets meaningfully colder. Brio prefers 70 but Brio is not paying the gas bill.

### 2.3 Water/sewer

Included in rent per the lease (paragraph 4(b)). No invoice. No action.

---

## Section 3 — Internet & insurance

### 3.1 Verizon Fios (account in Yael's name)

$79.99, billed 10-08. Same plan as September: 300/300 symmetrical, the cheapest tier that does not throttle on the 4K stuff Wren and I both use independently in the evenings.

Status: Wren Venmo'd $40 on 10-09, memo "fios oct". Settled. (Yael absorbs the $0.01 rounding short, as agreed in the original house rules §5.)

Cross-ref: see `verizon-fios-monthly.eml`.

### 3.2 Lemonade renter's insurance (joint policy, billed to Yael)

$14.18 on 10-15. No changes to coverage; same $25,000 personal property, $100,000 liability, $250 deductible profile we set up on 09-01. Wren Venmo'd $7.09 on 10-15, memo "lemonade". Settled.

Note: We had a small discussion about whether to up the personal property tier after Wren's monitor was stolen from the lobby on 10-22 — see Section 8.1 — but decided against it for now. The retailer reshipped, the policy held, and the new package locker (installed 10-29) addresses the underlying vulnerability.

---

## Section 4 — Streaming subscriptions

- Netflix ($22.99, Yael's account) — Yael absorbs in full this month per our standing arrangement, since Wren covers the Spotify Family that includes Camila and Alondra.
- Spotify Family ($19.99, Wren's account, includes Wren + Camila + Alondra) — Yael Venmo'd Wren $5 on 10-15, memo "spotify". Settled.
- No new subscriptions added in October. We talked about Mubi for one evening and did not act on it.

---

### 5.1 Visit 3 — Sat 10-11 09:00 ($130)

Wren paid Esperanza in cash from the kitchen-drawer envelope. Yael Venmo'd Wren $65 on 10-11, memo "cleaning 10/11". Settled. Notes: the apt was midway through Alondra's visit; Esperanza did the kitchen, both bathrooms (the bathroom ceiling was already repaired), the living room, and a quick pass on the bedrooms. Alondra flew back to Mexico City in the morning; I returned from Westchester (Naomi's knee surgery, Thursday 10-09) in the evening. Light meal at home, leftovers from the week; not formally tracked. Wren had done a full clean-out of the fridge in the afternoon, which I appreciated more than I said at the time. We sat at the kitchen table and amended the house rules (the toaster-incident-prompted clauses); see file 02.

Chiles en nogada, pomegranates in season. Wren went deep — toasted the nuts, made the picadillo from scratch, peeled the poblanos. Wren's treat — not split. If you ever find both machines tagged and need to do a load that day, the laundromat on Franklin a block south (Sudz) is reliable; I do not reimburse for those visits, but I am happy to drop a roll of quarters in your mailbox if you ever run out =E2=80=94 just text. =E2=80=A2 Smoke detectors were tested in August; chirping batteries should be reported. There are four detectors in 3B (kitchen, hallway, each bedroom) and one combined smoke/CO unit just inside the front door. The hallway one is the oldest =E2=80=94 if it is the one chirping, Joaqu=C3=ADn will probably swap the whole unit rather than just the 9-volt. Please do not take the battery out and forget to put it back; this is a New York City code item and the building inspection in October will look at every unit. =E2=80=A2 Trash pickup Mon/Thu 7 AM; recycling Wed. Bins live in the side alley off the stoop. The blue bin is mixed paper / cardboard, the green is metal/glass/plastic, and the black is landfill. A rug in the living room helps a lot; a rug under a bed helps even more. =E2=80=A2 The intercom buzzer at the front door is on its second life =E2=80=94 the original brass unit was replaced in 2019 with a networked panel, and most of the time it works exactly the way it looks like it should. **Maintainers:** Yael Strauss (primary maintainer), Wren Calderón (secondary)
**Last updated:** 2025-10-30 (revision 7)
**Document scope:** every appliance, kitchen tool, small-electric, cleaning tool, electronic, and shared bathroom/utility item currently in the apartment, plus a wishlist appendix and warranty notes.

> A small box at the top so we don't have to read the whole thing to find the new bits. Skim this, then go read the section.

## Document conventions

- This is a living document. Edits are made together, on a Sunday, with snacks.
- Proposed edits are written in *italics* for a week before they become real text.
- `[Y]:` and `[W]:` mark inline asides. They are not binding clauses; they are color.
- Strikethrough (`~~text~~`) means superseded text we kept around for memory.
- Every new clause carries a date stamp `(added YYYY-MM-DD)` so we can find it later.
- The *original* draft (v1.0, 2025-09-01) is preserved at `house/rules/house-rules-original-2025-09-01.md`. We did not delete anything.
- If a clause and a real-world reality disagree, we revise the clause, not the reality. Within reason.

---

## Section A — Money

A.1 Rent is **$3,400/month total**, split 50/50 — **$1,700 each** — due to Esra (landlord) on the **1st** via Zelle. Yael sends both halves from the joint Zelle memo line and Wren reimburses by Zelle on the same day or the day before. (Unchanged from v1.0.)

A.2 If either of us is going to be late on rent, we say so. (See also H.4, new.) Default is the 1st; latest acceptable is the 5th unless we've agreed otherwise.

A.3 Utilities are split 50/50. Account holder pays the full bill on receipt; the other roommate Venmos their share within 7 days. (Unchanged from v1.0; see Appendix 1 for the live monthly numbers in v1.1.)

A.4 Renter's insurance (Lemonade, **$14.18/month**) is on Yael's card; Wren Venmos **$7.09**.

A.5 Internet (Verizon Fios, **$79.99/month**) is on Yael's card; Wren Venmos **$40** flat (round number, our choice). The $0.005 per month over time is a rounding error we have agreed to ignore.

A.6 Streaming: Netflix **$22.99** (Yael's account, includes Wren); Spotify Family **$19.99** (Wren's account, covers Wren + Camila + Alondra). Yael Venmos Wren **$5/month** for Spotify share.

A.7 Cleaning service (Esperanza Mendez, every other Saturday): **$130/visit, split 50/50** = $65 each. Visits scheduled: 09-13, 09-27, 10-11, 10-25, etc. We tip in cash at the end of the year, not per-visit.

A.8 If a single grocery run, household supply, or shared restaurant night is small (<$30), we don't track it. We try to keep the long-run favors roughly even and we don't keep a ledger.

A.9 *(added 2025-10-12)* **Toaster precedent — explicitly not a precedent.** On 2025-09-29, Olu reimbursed Yael **$200** on Venmo for a $179.95 Smeg replacement bought 09-30 at Williams-Sonoma. The spread of **$20.05** was treated as a "we don't keep score" float (Wren bought the next two weeks of Sey Coffee from it). This is documented as an *example* of how a guest restitution went well; it is not a binding precedent for future incidents. See Section J for the actual policy. *[W]: olu felt awful, and the $20 turned into about three lattes and one croissant for me, fwiw.*

## Section B — Sound, sleep, and quiet hours

B.1 Quiet hours: **22:00 to 08:00 weeknights**, **23:00 to 09:00 weekends**. *(amended 2025-10-12)* — *amplified music in any common space ends by 22:00 on weeknights, 23:00 weekends.* "Amplified" here means living-room speaker, kitchen speaker, or anything plugged into a wall and pointed outward. Headphones at any time, of course.

B.2 ~~Acoustic instruments after 22:00 are fine if quiet.~~ — *(superseded 2025-10-12; see B.3.)*

B.3 *(amended 2025-10-12)* **Sentencia practice ends at 22:00 sharp. Equipment broken-down by 22:30. No exceptions for "just one more take."** We picked Wednesday partly because Yael has an editorial standing call Thursday morning at 09:00; the cutoff is structural, not a vibe.

B.4 Headphones in the living room before 09:00 weekends. Yael reads in bed; if Wren is up early they'll just be quiet. *(carry-over from v1.0; reaffirmed.)*

B.5 *(added 2025-10-12)* **Re: 2B (Mr. Nikolajević).** We've made friends with him. He's stopped Verdi-after-10 (he was playing *Don Carlo* and *Otello* loudly; one Saturday it was *La Traviata* at 23:30 and Yael wrote a polite note 09-25). Be courteous — he is older and slept poorly the week of 09-22 to 09-25. He calls Yael "the editor" and Wren "the bass player." *(He slid a tin of rakija under the door 09-26 with a courtly note. We have not opened it. We will have it on Halloween.)*

B.6 If practice is at the apartment (Wednesdays alternating; about two-thirds of practices land here in any given month), Wren tells Yael by Tuesday night. If Yael has a manuscript deadline, practice goes to Mei's place in Bushwick that week. *(carry-over from v1.0.)*

B.7 If a neighbor knocks, the host of the noise answers the door. We do not send each other to apologize for our own party.

## Section J — Guest damage, breakage, and restitution *(NEW in v1.1, added 2025-10-12)*

> See also: Appendix 4 (Breakage / restitution log), C.8–C.10, E.7, A.9.
> We didn't think we needed any of this. We were wrong. Live and learn.

**J.1 Host responsibility.** If your guest breaks something — appliance, dish, furniture, fixture — the *host* (the roommate who invited the guest) is responsible for either fronting the replacement or coordinating reimbursement. The non-host roommate should not have to chase anyone for money or replace anything themselves.

**J.2 24-hour notification window.** The host informs the other roommate **within 24 hours** of the breakage, ideally same-day. A text counts; a journal entry counts; a hallway "hey by the way" counts. What does not count: hoping the other roommate doesn't notice.

**J.3 7-day replacement window.** A like-for-like (or better) replacement is in the apartment **within 7 days**. If supply chain or sizing makes that impossible, we communicate the new ETA and pick an interim solution. (For the toaster, we had a temporary fill-in for ~48 hours: Yael's old 2-slice from her parents' attic, which her mom Naomi shipped down by request.)

**J.4 Photographic evidence preferred.** A photo of the broken thing — even a quick one — helps with: (a) Venmo memos, (b) a future "wait, when did this happen" question, and (c) any insurance claim if it ever rises to that. We are not building a case; we are building a record.

**J.5 Reimbursement flow: replace first, settle second.** The host (or guest) buys the replacement first. Reimbursement happens after — Venmo, Zelle, doesn't matter. **Don't make the broken-thing apartment limp along while we wait for money.** If the replacement is in the apartment by day 7, we are happy; the money is just paperwork.

**J.6 Worked example — the Smeg, 2025-09-28.**

> On **2025-09-28** Olu Adebayo (Wren's guest, drummer in Sentencia) dropped and broke the kitchen toaster while imitating a stage-dive he'd seen at a punk show. The toaster fell from the counter to the floor; the heating element cracked; the chrome face dented. *Awkwardness ensued.* Olu apologized profusely.
>
> On **2025-09-29** Olu Venmo'd Yael **$200** (memo: *"toaster atonement"*).
>
> On **2025-09-30** Wren bought a **Smeg 2-slice toaster** for **$179.95** at Williams-Sonoma (Brookfield Place store, in person; we wanted it in hand, not shipped to the lobby) and brought it home.
>
> Net: **+$20.05** in the shared float. We did not pocket it; Wren bought coffee at Sey for the next two weeks from it. By 10-12 the float was zeroed.
>
> *[W]: olu felt awful about this for like three days — he's banned from doing the worm in the kitchen but otherwise welcome.*

**J.7 Unprompted overcorrection gifts.** If a guest sends a follow-up gift on top of the reimbursement (see: the **Le Creuset mini-Dutch oven** Olu shipped to Yael the week of 10-06, retail ~$130, gift-wrapped, no receipt), we accept it with a thank-you text and we **do not counter-gift**. A counter-gift turns a small grace into a cycle. The thank-you text is enough. The mini-Dutch oven now lives on the open shelf above the stove, and it is genuinely a great pan.

**J.8 What this does *not* cover.** Pre-existing wear, structural building issues (the 09-22 leak; the 10-15 radiator knock), elevator outages (10-09), package theft from the lobby (10-22 monitor — that is the building's problem, not a guest-restitution thing). Section J is for in-apartment things broken by people we let in.

**J.9 Closing intent.** We trust each other. We trust our friends. This section exists so we don't have to *think* about a clear case — it's already decided. The toaster was clear. We want every future case to be this clear.

## Preamble

We moved in on the same day, separately, and we have known each other for exactly long enough to like each other and not yet long enough to know each other's worst habits. The intent of this document is not to police; it is to make the small frictions of cohabitation legible, so that when one of us is annoyed at something, we can point to the rule we wrote together when we were calm, instead of inventing a position in real time. It is also a reminder that we are sharing a galley kitchen, one bathroom, and a single radiator system that we hope works.

Where the rules are silent, default to: ask the other person, assume good faith, and write down whatever we decide so future-us has a record. We will revisit this document at least quarterly, or whenever something breaks (in the literal or relational sense).

## Section A — Money

### A.1 Rent

Rent is **$3,400/month total**, split 50/50 → **$1,700 each per month**, due on the 1st of each month. There is no proration for partial months in 2025 because we both moved in on the 1st; if a future month requires proration we will calculate it together.

### A.2 Rent payment

Each of us pays **Esra Polat** (landlord) directly, on or before the 1st of the month, via **Zelle** to the email address she provided in the lease packet (recorded in Appendix 2). Neither of us routes the other's share through our own account; one Zelle from each name keeps her bookkeeping clean and keeps us from accidentally becoming each other's accountant.

### A.3 Bills are split 50/50

All shared utilities and shared subscriptions are split **50/50**, regardless of whose name the account is in. The legal name on the bill is purely an artifact of who set it up first; it does not imply ownership of the cost.

### A.4 Shared bills and account-holder

| Bill | Account-holder | Approx monthly |
|---|---|---|
| ConEd (electric) | Yael | ~$80–$110 |
| National Grid (gas) | Wren | ~$20–$80 (heat-dependent) |
| Verizon Fios (internet) | Yael | $79.99 |
| Lemonade (renter's insurance, joint) | Yael | $14.18 |
| Esperanza Mendez (cleaning) | Alternates who books | $130/visit |

(See also Appendix 3 for the bill-account ownership matrix in long form.)

### A.5 Settling cadence

We use **Venmo within 7 days** of each invoice. Whoever's name is on the bill posts a screenshot or PDF of the invoice in our shared messaging thread the day it lands, with the split amount called out so the other person can pay without having to do arithmetic at 11 PM. If either of us is traveling or buried at work, an extension to 14 days is fine; longer than that, flag it.

### A.6 Streaming subscriptions

- **Netflix** ($22.99/mo) is on **Yael's** account; Wren has a profile.

For simplicity, we are not splitting Netflix and Spotify pro-rata against each other; instead **Yael venmos Wren $5/month** for the Spotify share, and Netflix is on Yael's tab. Reviewed if either of us cancels.

### A.7 Groceries and pantry staples

We **buy our own groceries**. The fridge has a Y shelf and a W shelf, marked with painter's tape (see C.1). Pantry staples — **olive oil, salt, coffee filters, paper towels, toilet paper, dish soap, sponges, trash bags¹** — are shared and bought by **whoever runs out first**. Informal balance-of-favors basis. **No tally.** If one of us starts feeling like the staples-buying is lopsided over a long stretch, we say so out loud rather than carrying a quiet ledger.

¹ The pantry-staples list is not exhaustive; obvious household consumables (parchment paper, ziploc bags, ice trays) fall in the same bucket. Specialty items (single-origin coffee beans, fancy olive oil, miso paste, anchovies) are personal unless explicitly offered.

### A.8 Alcohol and specialty items

**Not shared by default.** Wren keeps wine (orange and natural; the wine fridge is Wren's, on the W side of the kitchen). ## Section C — Kitchen & Food

### C.1 Fridge and pantry territory

The **top shelf is shared** and is the natural home of leftovers either of us is offering, plus eggs, plus the open bottle of soy sauce. Each of us has **one veggie drawer**. ### C.2 Dishes

**If you cook, you do not have to clean. If you didn't cook, you wash within 24 hours.** This includes the pots, the cutting boards, and the sink itself. The 24-hour clock starts at the time the meal ends, not the time you remember the meal happened. If both of us cooked separate meals at adjacent times, both of us clean our own.

Exceptions: if the cook makes a truly absurd mess (one of us once made bone broth and there was bone broth on the ceiling), the cook helps. We will know it when we see it.

### C.3 Sunday dinner ritual

We **alternate Sundays** as the cook:
- **Yael** cooks **vegetarian**.
- **Wren** cooks **omnivore**, and **Yael makes a side for herself** (usually a fish or bean version of whatever the protein is).

This is **optional, not mandatory**. We will not feel bad if a Sunday goes by and neither of us cooks; we will not feel beholden if one of us has plans. The point is to make the apartment feel like a home that has rituals in it, not to invent another obligation.

(Wren is allergic to **mango** — see C.4 — and Yael does not eat meat, but does eat fish. We have figured out how to braid this; nine weeks of dinners is plenty of practice.)

### C.4 Mango

**Wren is allergic to mango (oral allergy syndrome).** No mango in the kitchen unsupervised. If Yael wants mango sticky rice from the Thai place, she eats it at the kitchen table after warning Wren, washes hands and the cutting surface afterward, and the mango pit goes directly into the outdoor trash chute, not the kitchen bin. The kitchen knife she used does not go back into the block until it has been washed.

We are not panicking about cross-contamination — it's an OAS itch, not anaphylaxis — but it's avoidable, so we avoid it.

### C.5 Shared small appliances

The **toaster, kettle, French press, blender, and microwave** are shared. **Whoever broke it last replaces it.**

(Yael notes: "we will probably regret writing this in pen.")

The toaster is a 2-slot Cuisinart; Wren brought it from the previous apartment and is donating it to the household.
